meta.abstract:
ASML Holding N.V. occupies a singular position in the global technology supply chain: it is the sole manufacturer of extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography systems, the machines without which no leading-edge semiconductor can be fabricated at nodes below approximately 7 nanometers. That monopoly, assembled over four decades of compounding investment in laser physics, optics, metrology, and precision mechanics, has made ASML the indispensable upstream enabler of every advanced processor, AI accelerator, and high-bandwidth memory chip on the planet.

Founded in 1984 as a joint venture between Philips and ASM International in a leaky shed in Eindhoven — and relocated to Veldhoven, Netherlands, where it remains headquartered — ASML spent its first decade as a marginal stepper supplier before a decisive bet on deep-ultraviolet immersion technology and then on EUV elevated it to monopolist status. The 2013 acquisition of laser-light-source pioneer Cymer for approximately $2.5 billion, combined with a decades-long exclusive partnership with ZEISS Semiconductor Manufacturing Technology (SMT), in which ASML holds a minority stake of roughly 24 percent, cemented the technological and supply-chain barriers that no competitor has since been able to surmount.

By full-year 2025, ASML reported €32.7 billion in total net sales and €9.6 billion in net income at a gross margin of 52.8 percent, with a record year-end order backlog of €38.8 billion. The company shipped 48 EUV systems in 2025, generating €11.6 billion in EUV system revenue, up 39 percent year-over-year, while its installed-base management business — recurring revenue from upgrades, service, and holistic lithography software — contributed €8.2 billion. In Q1 2026 alone, ASML posted €8.8 billion in net sales at a 53 percent gross margin, prompting management to raise full-year 2026 guidance to €36–40 billion.

The dossier examines three interlocking strategic narratives: first, the transition from low-NA EUV (NXE:3600D / NXE:3800E) to High-NA EUV (EXE:5000 / EXE:5200) — the next-generation platform that enables sub-2-nanometer patterning and whose ramp with three foundry and logic customers is now under way; second, the China exposure problem, where U.S.-led export controls have curtailed DUV shipments to Chinese customers and reduced China's share of system revenue from approximately 36 percent in 2024 to roughly 19 percent in Q1 2026, forcing a geographic revenue re-mix toward AI-driven logic and DRAM capex in Taiwan, South Korea, and the United States; and third, ASML's longer-term ambition, articulated through a 2030 revenue scenario of €44–60 billion at gross margins of 56–60 percent, underpinned by AI infrastructure build-out, High-NA adoption, and the monetization of its growing installed base of more than 5,000 systems worldwide.

chapters.title: The Singular Machine: ASML's Strategic Position and Why It Cannot Be Replicated
chapters.body:
## The Rate-Limiting Node

Somewhere inside every artificial-intelligence accelerator, every advanced smartphone processor, and every high-bandwidth memory chip manufactured at the leading edge in 2026, there is a layer of circuitry that could not have been printed without a machine built in Veldhoven, Netherlands. No other machine exists. No other machine is coming. ASML Holding N.V. occupies a position in the global semiconductor supply chain that has no precise parallel in the history of industrial capitalism: absolute, uncontested, technically irreplicable monopoly over the one tool that determines whether the most advanced chips can be made at all.

That position expressed itself in numbers when ASML reported first-quarter 2026 results on April 16. [Net sales reached €8.8 billion](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/937966/000162828026025147/pressreleasefinancialresul.htm), gross margin held at 53 percent, and net income came in at €2.8 billion — a quarter that would rank as a full-year result for most semiconductor equipment companies. Management responded by raising full-year 2026 revenue guidance to €36–40 billion from a prior range of €34–39 billion, citing faster-than-expected capacity build-out by its three largest customers, all of them racing to supply the infrastructure layer of the AI economy. The guidance raise was not a routine revision. It was evidence that the demand signal driving ASML's order books — AI chip investment by TSMC, Samsung, and SK Hynix — had accelerated beyond what management had assumed at the start of the year.

## Three Narratives, One Machine

The dossier that follows is organized around three strategic narratives that together explain both ASML's current valuation and the risks that could disrupt it.

The first is **EUV monopoly monetization**. ASML shipped its first production Extreme Ultraviolet lithography system in 2018 after roughly two decades of development that consumed billions of euros and required co-investment from Intel, Samsung, and TSMC — customers who bought equity stakes in 2012 to secure supply and share risk. By 2025, EUV system sales had reached €11.6 billion, representing 48 machines at approximately €180 million apiece for the incumbent NXE:3800E platform. The barriers that protect this monopoly are not primarily financial; they are physical. EUV requires a 13.5-nanometer light source generated by firing a CO₂ laser at droplets of molten tin, a mirror and optical column manufactured exclusively by ZEISS SMT to nanometer tolerances, and a wafer stage with positional accuracy measured in picometers. Each system contains approximately 100,000 parts, takes roughly 18 months to build, and draws on supply chains that have no parallel anywhere on earth. Nikon and Canon, ASML's historical rivals, exited the EUV race before the first commercial machine shipped.

The second narrative is the **High-NA EUV generational transition**. ASML's EXE:5200 platform — the successor to the five research-phase EXE:5000 units seeded to TSMC, Intel, and Samsung in 2024 and early 2025 — introduces a numerical aperture of 0.55, against the current generation's 0.33, enabling single-exposure patterning below 8 nanometers. Two High-NA systems contributed over €4.1 billion of EUV revenue in Q1 2026 alone, signaling that the ramp was moving from qualification to early volume. With per-unit pricing estimated in the €300–400 million range, High-NA deepens the revenue per system while requiring customers to commit new process development resources — binding relationships that compound the installed-base lock-in already characteristic of the EUV franchise.

The third narrative is **China export-control exposure and geographic revenue re-mix**. China accounted for roughly 36 percent of ASML's net system sales in full-year 2024, almost entirely from Deep Ultraviolet immersion tools that U.S. export regulations have progressively restricted. By Q1 2026, China's share had fallen to approximately 19 percent. ASML's 2026 guidance bandwidth is explicitly designed to absorb further uncertainty; the structural argument is that lost China DUV revenue is being replaced by higher-margin EUV demand from AI-driven customers in Taiwan, Korea, and the United States — a mix shift that should expand gross margins even as the absolute China exposure contracts.

## Fouquet's Mandate

Christophe Fouquet, who became President and Chief Executive Officer on April 25, 2024, arrived at the top job from inside the EUV program itself. A French physicist who joined ASML in 2008 to lead EUV marketing and product management, he rose to Executive Vice President of EUV before becoming Chief Business Officer in 2022. His elevation was read by investors as a continuity signal: the critical task of the next four years is not financial engineering but the commercial execution of the High-NA transition, and Fouquet carried more direct product and customer intimacy around EUV than any alternative candidate could have offered. His predecessor Peter Wennink had shepherded the company through EUV's commercial birth; Fouquet's mandate is to scale its successor generation while managing China headwinds and sustaining the 2030 revenue scenario — €44–60 billion at 56–60 percent gross margins — that management articulated at its most recent investor day.

## What This Dossier Covers

The chapters that follow examine each dimension of that mandate in detail. The **Financials** section unpacks ASML's revenue trajectory, margin structure, capital returns, and valuation multiples against the semiconductor equipment peer group. The **Leadership** chapter profiles Fouquet and the Board of Management refresh completed at the April 2026 AGM. **Strategic Briefs** examine the five most consequential decisions shaping ASML's next decade — EUV ramp velocity, High-NA commercialization, China exposure management, the Mistral AI investment, and installed-base monetization. Each section is designed to answer a discrete question for the risk-adjusted investor: whether ASML's monopoly is durable, whether the High-NA transition is ahead of or behind schedule, and whether the 2030 revenue scenario reflects conservative guidance or optimistic extrapolation into an AI capex cycle that remains unproven in its duration.

chapters.title: From Philips Spinout to Global Monopolist: ASML's Forty-Year Ascent
chapters.body:
## The Leaky Shed on the Philips Campus

The company that would come to control the supply of every leading-edge semiconductor manufactured on earth began life in a building nobody wanted. On April 1, 1984, Philips N.V. and ASM International N.V. established ASM Lithography as a 50/50 joint venture in Eindhoven, Netherlands, charged with commercializing a wafer stepper prototype called the PAS 2000 that Philips had developed internally but could no longer afford to fund alone. The provisional facility on the Philips campus leaked when it rained. The two parent companies had different visions, different cultures, and a combined balance sheet that was inadequate for the task ahead. In 1985 the venture moved to a purpose-built factory in Veldhoven, just south of Eindhoven, a location that would eventually become one of the most consequential industrial campuses in the world.

The joint-venture structure was unstable by design. Philips spent the late 1980s and early 1990s selling down its stake, needing cash more than it needed equity in a capital-hungry photolithography company. ASM International lacked the balance sheet to absorb the full burden. By the mid-1990s the resolution was structural rather than incremental: ASML — the name formalized as the company's standalone brand — listed on Euronext Amsterdam and Nasdaq in 1995, a fully independent public company with the capital markets as its new backer. The leaky shed had, in a decade, become a publicly traded manufacturer competing for the most technically demanding contracts in global industry.

## The DUV Battleground

For the next fifteen years, ASML fought a two-front war it was not expected to win. Nikon and Canon, backed by Japan's industrial ecosystem, dominant in the stepper market, and deeply resourced, set the competitive baseline. The question was whether a Dutch spinout with no optical heritage could displace incumbents with decades of precision manufacturing expertise.

ASML's answer was strategic rather than brute-force. Rather than attempting to replicate Nikon's vertically integrated optical column in-house, ASML chose partnership and licensing. The critical relationship was with Carl Zeiss SMT in Oberkochen, Germany, which supplied the optical columns — the precision lens assemblies that focused light onto the wafer. By licensing rather than internalizing, ASML traded short-term margin for long-term exclusivity, and the exclusivity eventually became the moat. Zeiss SMT's optics were world-class; ASML's systems integration around them was world-class. The combination proved superior.

The acquisition of Silicon Valley Group in 2001 accelerated ASML's installed-base scale in the United States, giving it customer relationships and field service infrastructure that Nikon and Canon struggled to match outside Japan. By the mid-2000s, ASML had established leadership in 193-nanometer deep-ultraviolet immersion lithography, a technique in which a film of water between the lens and the wafer effectively shortened the working wavelength and extended the resolution limit of existing optical infrastructure. The immersion gamble — contested internally, dismissed initially by rivals — bought the industry nearly a decade of additional Moore's Law progress without requiring EUV. It also built ASML an installed base of several thousand systems, creating a recurring service and upgrade revenue stream that would later underpin the company's financial resilience through cyclical downturns.

By 2010, Nikon's share of the advanced lithography market had contracted materially. Canon had largely retreated from leading-edge. ASML had not merely survived the DUV era — it had reshaped the competitive landscape so thoroughly that its two Japanese rivals would never meaningfully re-engage.

## The Customer Co-Investment Turning Point

EUV lithography had been a research aspiration since the late 1990s, when a U.S. government-backed consortium called EUV LLC — which included Intel, Motorola, and others — began exploring 13.5-nanometer extreme ultraviolet light as the path beyond 193nm immersion. ASML took on the development baton, but by the early 2010s the cost trajectory had grown beyond what ASML's own balance sheet could support while also funding the DUV business. The solution was structurally novel: ASML asked its own customers to become its investors.

In 2012, Intel, Samsung, and TSMC collectively paid approximately €3.85 billion for approximately 23 percent of ASML's equity. In exchange, they secured preferential access to EUV supply and shared the development risk. It was an arrangement without modern precedent in the capital equipment industry — chipmakers essentially subsidizing the R&D of their own tool supplier, converting a supplier relationship into a technology partnership. The arrangement also gave ASML the financial runway to accelerate EUV development without constant capital market pressure, and it gave the three largest logic and memory manufacturers an incentive to make EUV succeed: their own money was in the outcome.

The stakes in the 2012 structure were subsequently reduced as ASML bought back shares and the partners rotated positions, but the strategic signal was permanent. ASML was no longer merely a vendor. It was a co-development partner to the foundry industry's most important participants.

## Cymer and the Supply Chain Lock

The following year, ASML moved to eliminate the largest remaining external dependency in EUV's supply chain. Cymer, headquartered in San Diego, California, had developed the laser-produced plasma technology that generated EUV light by firing a high-powered CO2 laser at droplets of molten tin, causing a plasma discharge that emitted 13.5-nanometer radiation. Cymer was the dominant light-source supplier for both DUV excimer lasers and EUV development systems, and as long as it remained independent, ASML's EUV roadmap was hostage to a third-party supplier's technology choices and financial priorities.

ASML acquired Cymer in 2013 for approximately $2.5 billion. The transaction accomplished two things simultaneously: it consolidated full intellectual property control over the EUV light source within ASML, and it gave ASML the engineering talent and San Diego R&D infrastructure to push EUV source power — then an acute bottleneck — from tens of watts toward the hundreds of watts needed for production throughput. Over the following decade, Cymer's engineers, now operating as ASML's light source division, drove source power from roughly 80 watts in early production tools to above 500 watts in the NXE:3800E, a sixfold increase that was as responsible for EUV's commercial viability as any optical or mechanical innovation.

## The Commercialization Arc

The first EUV tool ASML shipped for external use was the NXE:3100, delivered to the Belgian research institute IMEC in 2010. It was a research instrument, not a production machine — throughput was measured in single-digit wafers per hour and the light source was intermittently unreliable — but it proved the concept in an environment with access to real process engineers and real chip patterns.

Production-class EUV arrived gradually. ASML shipped the NXE:3300B to TSMC and Samsung beginning around 2016, followed by the NXE:3400B in 2017 and 2018. These were the tools that allowed chipmakers to learn EUV integration — to master overlay, to handle the sensitivity of EUV resists, to manage the complexity of pellicle-protected reticles — before committing the technology to volume production. TSMC moved first. In 2019 the company used EUV on its N7+ node, the first time the technology appeared in commercially shipped silicon: the Apple A13 Bionic was among the first consumer chips to contain layers patterned by an ASML EUV machine.

The ramp that followed was steep. The NXE:3600D raised throughput to 160 wafers per hour; the NXE:3800E reached 220 wafers per hour upon release and climbed to 230 with a productivity enhancement package in early 2026. ASML shipped 48 EUV systems in full-year 2025, generating €11.6 billion in EUV revenue — a 39 percent increase over 2024 — from a product line that had generated essentially no revenue fifteen years earlier.

## Wennink to Fouquet: EUV's Second Chapter

Peter Wennink had served as ASML's chief executive for twelve years, a tenure that encompassed the Cymer acquisition, the 2012 customer co-investment, and the entire arc of EUV commercialization from laboratory curiosity to the world's most valuable production machine. He stepped down on April 25, 2024, alongside chief technology officer Martin van den Brink, the engineer most closely associated with EUV's long development. Their simultaneous departure was choreographed rather than abrupt — a generational handoff that ASML had signaled to investors well in advance.

Christophe Fouquet, a French physicist who had joined ASML in 2008 and spent years running EUV product management before ascending to chief business officer, took the chief executive role. His elevation was read by analysts as a signal of product continuity: unlike a financial or operational executive brought in to optimize a mature business, Fouquet carried the intimate technical and customer knowledge that the complexity of the High-NA transition demanded.

The timing was deliberate. In 2024 ASML shipped its first EXE:5000 High-NA EUV system — a machine with a numerical aperture of 0.55 versus the 0.33 of existing low-NA tools, enabling single-exposure patterning at feature sizes that would otherwise require two or three multi-patterning steps. The EXE:5000, priced in the range of €300–400 million per unit, went to TSMC, Intel, and Samsung for process qualification. Fouquet inherited not merely an ongoing EUV franchise but the launch of its successor generation — forty years after two parent companies gambled on a leaky shed in Eindhoven.

chapters.title: The Product Architecture: EUV, High-NA, DUV, and the Holistic Lithography Ecosystem
chapters.body:
## The NXE Platform: Low-NA EUV at Commercial Scale

The machine that transformed modern chip manufacturing into a natural monopoly measures roughly the size of a city bus and contains approximately 100,000 individually engineered components. ASML's NXE platform — the low-NA EUV product family operating at a numerical aperture of 0.33 — has been in volume production since 2018 and by 2025 had become the rate-limiting tool in every sub-5nm logic node on the planet.

The physics begin with a CO₂ laser firing at 50,000 tin droplets per second inside a vacuum chamber. Each collision vaporizes the tin into a plasma that emits photons at 13.5 nanometers — extreme ultraviolet light, so energetic that it is absorbed by virtually every known material including air itself. The entire optical path must operate in hard vacuum. The illumination system routes that light through a series of multilayer mirrors, each polished at ZEISS SMT's facility in Oberkochen, Germany, to tolerances measured in fractions of a nanometer. Those mirrors — manufactured nowhere else in the world — focus the beam onto a reticle (mask) containing the circuit pattern, which is then projected at a 4x reduction ratio onto the silicon wafer below. The wafer stage positions each exposure field with picometer-scale accuracy at speeds that allow throughput of 220 to 230 wafers per hour.

The current flagship, the NXE:3800E, reached its rated 220 wafers-per-hour specification in 2024 and received a Productivity Enhancement Package — designated PEP-1E — in Q1 2026 that lifted throughput to 230 wafers per hour without degrading overlay performance. Its predecessor, the NXE:3600D, served as the principal production workhorse for early EUV adoption at TSMC's N7+ and N5 nodes before the 3800E displaced it at leading-edge fabs. In-band light source power runs at approximately 250 watts, a figure that determines the fundamental ceiling on throughput and represents decades of incremental engineering by Cymer — the San Diego light-source operation ASML acquired in 2013 for approximately $2.5 billion.

ASML shipped 48 NXE systems in full-year 2025 at an average selling price of approximately €180 million each, generating €11.6 billion in EUV system revenue — a 39 percent increase over 2024. At that scale, every wafer manufactured at TSMC's N3 node, Samsung's 3GAE process, and SK Hynix's advanced DRAM passed beneath an NXE optical column. There is no substitute.

## The EXE Platform: High-NA EUV and the Sub-8nm Frontier

If the NXE platform built ASML's monopoly, the EXE platform is designed to sustain it for the following decade. High-NA EUV raises the numerical aperture from 0.33 to 0.55 — a shift that narrows the minimum resolvable feature from roughly 13nm to below 8nm in a single exposure, eliminating the costly and yield-penalizing multi-patterning schemes that low-NA EUV requires at the most advanced nodes.

The optical geometry change is not incremental. To achieve 0.55 NA, ASML's engineers adopted an anamorphic lens architecture, meaning the optical magnification differs between the x and y axes: 8x in one direction, 4x in the other. This change — necessary because a symmetric 0.55 NA lens at useful field sizes would require mirror diameters physically impossible to manufacture to optical tolerance — carries a significant consequence for chip manufacturers. The new EXE reticle format covers only half the area of a conventional EUV mask field. Chipmakers must either split their designs across two exposures (called field-stitching) or redesign layouts to fit the new exposure window, both of which require substantial process integration investment. That investment becomes a further switching cost; a customer who has qualified processes on EXE equipment has no rational path to a competitor that does not exist.

ASML completed shipment of five EXE:5000 systems to three foundry and logic customers — widely understood within the industry to be TSMC, Intel, and Samsung — by the end of Q1 2025. These were research-phase systems intended for process development rather than production. Production transitioned to the successor EXE:5200 from Q2 2025 onward. Average selling prices for High-NA systems are estimated at €300 to €400 million per unit, roughly double the NXE:3800E list price, reflecting the step increase in optical complexity and the ZEISS SMT mirror sets required for 0.55 NA. Two High-NA systems contributed to Q1 2026 EUV revenue of over €4.1 billion in that single quarter alone, an early signal of volume economics beginning to register.

For the logic roadmap, High-NA matters acutely at the sub-2nm nodes — Intel's 14A, TSMC's N2P and beyond, Samsung's competing offerings. At these geometries, low-NA EUV with multi-patterning becomes economically and yield-structurally inadequate. High-NA single-exposure patterning is not merely preferable; at some feature dimensions, it is the only manufacturable path.

## The TWINSCAN DUV Line: The Workhorse Beneath the Glamour

EUV occupies the strategic summit, but DUV lithography — deep ultraviolet, using 193nm ArF or 248nm KrF light — still constitutes the physical majority of exposure steps in every chip fabricated anywhere in the world. ASML's TWINSCAN product family covers this range.

The NXT:2100i and NXT:2050i represent the advanced tier: ArF immersion systems that use water as an optical medium between lens and wafer to achieve effective wavelengths below the physical 193nm limit, enabling multi-patterning schemes at nodes from 65nm down below 10nm. These tools handle the non-critical layers in leading-edge logic and support the entirety of mainstream DRAM and NAND fabrication. Dry KrF and dry ArF systems serve mature nodes — automotive, analog, RF, power semiconductors — at substantially lower average selling prices.

China's relevance to DUV is both commercial and geopolitical. Chinese customers — SMIC, Hua Hong, and a range of capacity-expanding fabs — represented approximately 36 percent of ASML net system sales in full-year 2024, with the preponderance of that exposure in DUV immersion systems. Progressive tightening of U.S. export control regulations — coordinated between Washington and The Hague — has progressively restricted advanced immersion DUV shipments to Chinese customers. By Q1 2026, China's share of net system sales had fallen to approximately 19 percent. Basic dry DUV systems face fewer export constraints and continue to ship, as does service revenue on the existing China installed base, but the immersion tier has been effectively closed for leading Chinese foundry customers. ASML's 2026 guidance bandwidth of €36–40 billion is explicitly sized to absorb further China uncertainty.

## Metrology, Inspection, and the YieldStar Portfolio

Lithography systems print patterns; metrology systems verify that the printing was accurate. ASML's YieldStar optical metrology platform uses diffraction-based measurements to quantify overlay error — the misalignment between successive patterning layers — and critical-dimension (CD) accuracy across the wafer. As node geometries have shrunk below 10nm, overlay tolerances have compressed into the single-digit nanometer range; even sub-nanometer misalignment at EUV layers can cause catastrophic yield loss at the interconnect levels that follow.

The HMI e-beam inspection platform provides a complementary capability: high-resolution electron-beam imaging that detects defects too small for optical detection. Both YieldStar and HMI platforms are sold to the same foundry and memory customers as ASML's scanners, creating a portfolio relationship that deepens commercial intimacy with key accounts.

## Holistic Lithography: The Software Lock-in

The most durable competitive advantage in ASML's portfolio may not be hardware at all. Holistic Lithography is ASML's software-and-services platform that co-optimizes the three principal variables governing patterning fidelity: the illumination source, the reticle (mask) design, and the scanner parameters. By ingesting metrology data from YieldStar, design data from the customer's EDA tools, and real-time performance data from the scanner itself, Holistic Lithography applies computational corrections — source-mask optimization, aberration corrections, focus and dose tuning — that can recover yield without hardware intervention.

The commercial model is structurally recurring. Customers pay subscription or service-contract fees for access to the Holistic Lithography software stack and the associated computational infrastructure. Combined with the broader installed-base management segment — scanner upgrades, optical column improvements, service contracts — this recurring business generated €8.2 billion in 2025, growing faster than the systems business and carrying margins that are less sensitive to new-system manufacturing cost fluctuations. Installed-base management now constitutes approximately 25 percent of total ASML revenue, a figure management expects to grow as the global installed base of more than 5,000 systems ages and generates increasingly complex upgrade and service requirements.

The lock-in mechanism is self-reinforcing. A customer operating both EXE High-NA scanners and YieldStar metrology tools, running Holistic Lithography software, has integrated ASML's control loop into the most sensitive process steps in its fab. Extracting that stack is not an equipment procurement decision; it is a multi-year process re-qualification program measured in hundreds of millions of dollars and substantial yield risk.

## Product Roadmap: From EXE:5200 to Hyper-NA

The EXE:5200 entered customer fabs from Q2 2025 and represents the first High-NA system configured for production-intent process qualification, rather than the research-phase EXE:5000 it superseded. An EXE:5400 — a further throughput and overlay improvement on the 0.55 NA platform — is anticipated as the natural successor, maintaining the generational cadence ASML has followed within both NXE and prior DUV families.

The longer-term conceptual program is Hyper-NA: a notional platform operating above 0.55 NA that would require fundamental changes to wafer stage design and potentially the reticle-to-wafer geometry. Hyper-NA remains in early research and has not been assigned a product timeline; it is best understood as ASML's signal to customers and capital markets that the EUV roadmap does not terminate at 0.55 NA.

Underpinning every product generation is an intellectual property architecture that encompasses approximately 38,000 patents across 32 jurisdictions. That portfolio covers light source physics, optical column geometry, wafer stage mechanics, reticle handling, vacuum engineering, and metrology algorithms — effectively the complete engineering domain of lithographic patterning. No entrant could reproduce the product by licensing around the edges; the patents represent accumulated invention across four decades of R&D expenditure, including approximately €4.7 billion invested in research and development in 2025 alone. The IP moat is not a complement to the physical moat. They are the same moat.

chapters.title: Revenue Trajectory, Margin Architecture, and Capital Structure
chapters.body:
## From Trough to Record: The Revenue Trajectory That Defied the Cycle

ASML's financial history across the first half of this decade reads less like a traditional semiconductor equipment company and more like a platform software franchise navigating a single severe cyclical interruption. Full-year 2020 revenue came in at roughly €14 billion as the pandemic reshuffled capital spending priorities. By 2022, that figure had expanded to approximately €21.2 billion, driven by a post-pandemic capex surge across logic and memory customers. The acceleration continued into 2023, when net sales reached €27.6 billion — a record at the time — as TSMC, Samsung, and SK Hynix pushed aggressive EUV deployments in tandem with a memory capacity build that, in retrospect, had already begun to overshoot demand.

The 2024 step-down followed precisely that overshoot. DRAM manufacturers, having burned through HBM-related budget earlier than planned, pulled back sharply on new system commitments. Simultaneously, Chinese customers had spent 2022 and 2023 front-loading DUV immersion orders ahead of anticipated export restriction tightening — a rational acceleration that effectively borrowed from future demand. When those restrictions tightened further and Chinese fab expansion plans moderated, the artificial 2022–2023 volume support evaporated. ASML's full-year 2024 net sales declined from the 2023 peak to approximately €28.3 billion, a contraction of roughly 2 percent that surprised analysts who had expected the company's backlog to provide more durable insulation.

The recovery proved sharper than consensus expected. Full-year 2025 net sales reached €32.7 billion, a 15.5 percent increase over 2024, [representing the second consecutive annual record after adjusting for the 2024 interruption](https://www.asml.com/en/news/press-releases/2026/q4-2025-financial-results). The demand catalyst was unmistakable: artificial intelligence infrastructure investment had shifted the order intake profile decisively toward leading-edge logic and HBM memory, both of which require ASML's highest-value EUV systems. Following Q1 2026 results of €8.8 billion in net sales, management raised its full-year 2026 revenue guidance to €36–40 billion, representing a midpoint of €38 billion — roughly 16 percent above the 2025 outturn.

## Decomposing 2025: Three Revenue Engines at Different Speeds

ASML's 2025 top line decomposed across three distinct revenue streams, each carrying different growth rates, margin profiles, and cyclical sensitivity.

EUV system sales contributed €11.6 billion in 2025, representing 48 systems shipped and a 39 percent increase over 2024. The average selling price of a low-NA NXE:3800E system approached €180 million at list, though individual transactions reflect negotiated terms and configuration choices. By Q1 2026, the revenue mix had already begun shifting toward High-NA EUV: two EXE:5200 systems contributed more than €4.1 billion of EUV revenue in the quarter alone, implying average selling prices in the €300–400 million range per unit — materially above low-NA equivalents and consistent with the mechanical and optical complexity of the 0.55-NA platform.

DUV system sales — the residual after subtracting EUV and installed-base management from the €32.7 billion total — remained a meaningful contributor, though export controls had substantially changed the customer mix. Chinese fabs, which had accounted for approximately 36 percent of net system sales in 2024, fell to roughly 19 percent of the mix by Q1 2026 as restrictions curtailed advanced DUV immersion shipments. The customer gap was progressively filled by AI-driven logic demand at TSMC, Samsung, and Intel, which required both DUV tools for mature patterning layers and EUV tools for critical layers.

Installed-base management contributed €8.2 billion in 2025, constituting roughly 25 percent of total revenue. This segment — comprising service contracts, scanner upgrades, optical column enhancements, and Holistic Lithography software subscriptions — operates over an installed base of more than 5,000 systems globally accumulated across four decades of shipments. It is the fastest-growing and most margin-resilient component of the business: unlike system sales, installed-base revenue is not subject to customer acceptance timing, does not compress sharply in capex down cycles, and carries software economics that approximate recurring revenue. ASML's 2030 scenario planning assumes this segment grows faster than the systems business, providing a higher-quality earnings floor as the cycle matures.

A critical accounting feature shapes how all three streams translate into reported quarterly revenue. ASML recognizes system revenue upon customer acceptance, not shipment. Because EUV systems take months to install and qualify after physical delivery, and because customers complete acceptance testing at their own pace, revenue tends to cluster in Q4 as year-end deadlines concentrate acceptance events. This acceptance-driven cadence introduces genuine lumpiness into the quarterly progression — a company with a growing backlog may report soft interim quarters while shipments accumulate — and amplifies the significance of any single large customer acceptance event.

## The Margin Staircase: From 51 to 60 Percent

ASML's gross margin trajectory tells the story of a business engineering its own revenue mix shift in real time.

| Period | Gross Margin | Key Driver |
|---|---|---|
| FY 2024 | ~51.3% | Memory cycle trough, China DUV mix |
| FY 2025 | 52.8% | EUV mix shift, installed-base growth |
| Q1 2026 | 53.0% | High-NA ramp commencement |
| 2026 Guidance | 51–53% | High-NA cost headwinds in ramp phase |
| 2030 Target | 56–60% | High-NA scale, software/service mix |

The improvement from 2024 to 2025 reflected two simultaneous forces: the rising share of EUV within system sales (EUV systems carry higher gross margins than DUV at comparable revenue recognition stages), and the structural growth of installed-base management as a proportion of total revenue. Service and software revenue, by ASML's own description, carries margins above the corporate average, so each incremental percentage point of installed-base share mechanically improves the blended margin.

The 2026 guidance range of 51–53 percent represents a near-term constraint rather than deterioration. High-NA EUV systems, despite their materially higher average selling prices, currently carry manufacturing cost headwinds as ASML climbs the production learning curve on the EXE:5200. The optical column — a bespoke anamorphic design manufactured by ZEISS SMT — is more complex and more expensive to produce per unit than the symmetric optics in low-NA systems, and yields on both the optics and the wafer stage will improve with volume. Management's 2030 margin target of 56–60 percent assumes that the High-NA learning curve normalizes, that installed-base revenue continues to grow as a share of the mix, and that Holistic Lithography software progressively carries higher recurring revenue characteristics. At 60 percent gross margin, ASML would rank among the highest-margin industrial companies in the world — closer to KLA Corporation's current ~61 percent than to the 51 percent trough of 2024.

## Capital Returns, R&D Allocation, and the Mistral Wager

ASML's capital allocation in 2025 illustrated the unusual position of a company that is simultaneously the world's most complex industrial R&D program and a cash return machine operating at software-level margins.

R&D expenditure reached approximately €4.7 billion in 2025, roughly 14 percent of net sales. This is not discretionary spending — it funds the next EUV generation, High-NA manufacturing scale-up, Holistic Lithography software development, and the early-stage research into Hyper-NA (0.75+ NA) that will eventually follow EXE:5200. Against that backdrop, ASML returned €8.5 billion to shareholders through dividends and share repurchases — a capital return figure that exceeded its entire R&D budget by nearly €3.8 billion and underscores how freely the business generates cash relative to its reinvestment requirements.

Free cash flow generation on a trailing basis reached approximately €10.4 billion as of early 2026, supporting a free cash flow yield of approximately 1.6 percent against a market capitalization in the €616–629 billion range. That yield is low in absolute terms — well below the S&P 500's median FCF yield of approximately 4 percent — but consistent with the valuation premium attached to a business with a structural monopoly, multi-year backlog visibility, and secular demand tailwinds. Share repurchases have reduced outstanding shares to approximately 385 million as of early 2026, with the decline modestly accretive to per-share metrics including the €24.73 basic earnings per share reported for full-year 2025.

The most unusual capital deployment in the 2025 cycle was ASML's approximately €1.3 billion (~$1.5 billion) strategic investment in Mistral AI, which made ASML the French AI company's largest shareholder and secured a board seat. The rationale spanned two dimensions: operational (accelerating AI-driven process optimization within ASML's Holistic Lithography platform) and strategic (an expression of ASML's thesis that European AI capability is both commercially important to its long-term operating environment and likely to remain underinvested without anchoring industrial sponsorship). The investment consumed a meaningful share of a single year's free cash flow and will be scrutinized against the operational synergies it delivers as Holistic Lithography evolves.

## Balance Sheet Architecture: Conservative Leverage, Extraordinary Backlog

ASML's balance sheet reflects a deliberate choice to operate with minimal leverage in an industry where customer concentration and geopolitical exposure could, in principle, create acute revenue stress.

The debt-to-equity ratio stood at approximately 0.13 as of year-end 2025, reflecting modest borrowings against a substantial equity base. The current ratio of approximately 1.36 indicated adequate liquidity coverage of near-term obligations. This conservatism is not simply risk aversion — it reflects a business model in which the most capital-intensive items (R&D, manufacturing tooling, customer support infrastructure) are funded entirely from internally generated cash flow, leaving the balance sheet unencumbered as a strategic option against further geopolitical disruption or acquisition opportunities.

The most consequential balance sheet item, however, is not leverage but backlog. ASML ended 2025 with a record order backlog of €38.797 billion, supported by full-year 2025 net bookings of €28.035 billion. Q4 2025 net bookings alone reached €13.158 billion, of which €7.4 billion was EUV — a single-quarter figure that, if annualized, would exceed total EUV system sales for all of 2024. At the midpoint of 2026 guidance (€38 billion), the year-end 2025 backlog represented approximately 12 months of forward revenue coverage, meaning ASML entered 2026 with full-year revenue effectively pre-committed from existing orders before writing a single new contract.

## The Transparency Trade-Off: Discontinuing Quarterly Order Disclosure

One of the more consequential and underappreciated financial communication decisions of 2025 was ASML's announcement that it would discontinue quarterly net bookings disclosure beginning in Q2 2025, shifting to annual-only reporting of order intake data.

For years, the quarterly bookings figure had served as the primary short-term demand signal watched by sell-side analysts and the basis for many earnings model adjustments. When ASML accidentally published its Q3 2024 results a day early — revealing below-consensus order intake — the stock declined approximately 30 percent from its peak in the weeks that followed, as the market reacted to the demand signal as a read-through to the entire semiconductor equipment sector.

Management's argument for discontinuation was that quarterly order volatility created misleading demand signals: EUV systems are large, long-lead items, and a single quarter's booking figure could swing dramatically based on whether one or two large orders arrived before or after a quarter-end. Annual figures, management argued, would better reflect the structural demand environment.

The practical effect was a reduction in near-term model transparency that made short-term earnings variance harder to forecast. Analysts who had built quarterly models anchored to bookings data were required to rely more heavily on qualitative guidance and customer capex announcements. Whether this contributed to stock volatility is difficult to disentangle from the concurrent geopolitical and macro signals — but the elimination of a historically closely watched leading indicator during an already uncertain period for China-exposed revenues amplified uncertainty for investors building twelve-month models. The move also reflected a form of strategic confidence: a company that believes its backlog and secular demand narrative are strong enough that quarterly booking noise is more likely to mislead than inform.

chapters.title: How the Market Prices a Monopoly: Multiples, Scenarios, and What the Stock Implies
chapters.body:
## A Premium Built in Veldhoven

At roughly $1,600 per share on the Nasdaq as of late May 2026, ASML Holding trades at a valuation that has no peer in the semiconductor equipment industry and few analogues in industrial manufacturing. A trailing price-to-earnings ratio of approximately 53–54x, a forward P/E of 40–41x, an EV/EBITDA of 41–42x, and an EV/Sales of 15.7x collectively describe a company the market is pricing not as a cyclical capital-equipment vendor but as something closer to a platform software franchise with irreplaceable infrastructure characteristics. Understanding whether that judgment is correct — or merely premature — requires decomposing what the current multiple is actually pricing in.

The stock's own five-year history offers the first reference point. Through the early EUV commercialization phase, ASML's P/E typically ranged from 35x to 45x, compressing toward the lower bound during capex-cycle troughs and expanding above 45x during periods of strong bookings momentum and bullish AI sentiment. The 53–54x trailing multiple observed in May 2026 sits above that band, sustained by a combination of factors that were not present in prior cycles: a record backlog of €38.8 billion, a High-NA product line with no competitive equivalent, and an AI-driven capex acceleration that has broadened the customer base of EUV demand beyond foundry logic into DRAM and advanced packaging. The [free cash flow yield of approximately 1.6%](https://stockanalysis.com/stocks/asml/statistics/) at current prices is consistent with a long-duration compounding asset rather than a value opportunity — and consistent with a market implying that today's earnings per share are not the right denominator for assessing intrinsic worth.

## Peers in the Rearview Mirror

ASML's premium to its semiconductor equipment peers is structural, not anomalous. The table below compares ASML against the four largest publicly traded equipment companies, using May 2026 figures.

| Company | Market Cap (USD) | Trailing P/E | Forward P/E | EV/EBITDA | EV/Sales | Gross Margin | 1-Yr Rev Growth |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **ASML** | ~$620B | ~53–54x | ~40–41x | ~41–42x | ~15.7x | 52.8% | +15.5% |
| **Applied Materials (AMAT)** | ~$170B | ~21x | ~19x | ~16x | ~5.5x | ~47.5% | ~8% |
| **Lam Research (LRCX)** | ~$80B | ~22x | ~20x | ~16x | ~5.3x | ~47.5% | ~22% |
| **KLA Corporation (KLAC)** | ~$100B | ~25x | ~22x | ~19x | ~8.5x | ~61% | ~18% |
| **Tokyo Electron (TEL)** | ~$68B | ~24x | ~21x | ~16x | ~4.6x | ~46% | ~17% |

The ASML-to-peer premium on EV/Sales — roughly 2–3x on a relative basis — is the clearest expression of what the market is paying for monopoly positioning. AMAT, Lam, KLA, and TEL are competitive businesses operating in markets where customers choose between multiple qualified suppliers; ASML is not. The reticle of choice for every sub-7nm logic node, every advanced DRAM layer, every future chiplet architecture is an ASML EUV scanner. That pricing power — reflected in EUV average selling prices above €180 million for low-NA and an estimated €300–400 million for High-NA systems — is the justification for the EV/Sales premium.

KLA comes closest on gross margin at approximately 61%, but trades at a meaningful valuation discount because it competes in metrology and process control markets where Onto Innovation and Hitachi High-Tech provide credible alternatives. The 35x ASML-to-KLA P/E premium reflects the difference between a near-monopoly and a dominant competitor. Premium contraction to a KLA-equivalent 25x forward P/E — were ASML to lose a major customer, suffer an EUV yield crisis, or face a credible entrant — would imply a share price in the range of $900–1,000 at current forward earnings estimates, a decline of approximately 40 percent from May 2026 levels.

## What $1,600 Per Share Actually Implies

A ten-year discounted cash flow model built from ASML's current free cash flow of approximately €10.4 billion ($11.4 billion at current EUR/USD) and a 10 percent weighted average cost of capital reveals the magnitude of the growth path embedded in the price. To justify a roughly $620 billion market capitalization with a 3 percent terminal growth assumption, the model requires ASML to grow free cash flow at approximately 13–15 percent annually for the next decade. That trajectory maps to total revenues approaching €70 billion by the mid-2030s — a figure that would represent more than a doubling of the 2025 base and implies ASML capturing the majority of the value created by each successive semiconductor node transition from High-NA through whatever follows.

Stated differently, the market is not pricing in ASML's 2030 scenario range — it is pricing in the view that the 2030 scenario *floor* materializes and that the growth cycle continues well beyond. The €44 billion base case for 2030 would represent only a six percent compound annual growth rate from 2025, which at a compressed multiple of 30–32x forward earnings would imply a stock price near current levels by 2030 with minimal capital appreciation over the intervening four years. To justify buying at $1,600 today, an investor must believe the $60 billion scenario — or something close to it — is the central case, not the ceiling.

## Scoring the PEG

ASML's price-to-earnings-growth ratio bridges the gap between multiple and growth rate. At a forward P/E of approximately 40–41x and a consensus 2025–2027 earnings per share compound annual growth rate of roughly 19–21 percent — extrapolating from FY2025 basic EPS of €24.73 toward analyst central estimates near €36–38 by FY2027 — the PEG ratio settles at approximately 2.0x. By the conventional rule-of-thumb that a PEG below 1x signals undervaluation, ASML screens as expensive in absolute terms.

Against peers, the picture is more nuanced. AMAT and Lam Research carry PEGs in the 1.3–1.6x range; KLA, with its superior gross margins and more defensive revenue mix, trades near 1.5x. Tokyo Electron, benefiting from yen weakness and strong domestic government support, is closer to 1.3x. ASML's 2.0x PEG premium over the peer group reflects three things that a growth rate alone does not capture: the structural absence of competition, the multi-year backlog providing earnings visibility that reduces discount rate, and the terminal value optionality embedded in High-NA, which is still in the earliest innings of its commercial deployment.

## Bull, Base, and Bear

| Scenario | 2026 Revenue | Net Margin | Forward EPS (USD) | P/E Applied | Implied Share Price |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Bull** | €40B (guidance top) | ~31% | ~$43 | ~48x | ~$2,050–2,100 |
| **Base** | €38B (guidance midpoint) | ~29% | ~$37–39 | ~40x | ~$1,480–1,560 |
| **Bear** | €34–35B | ~26% | ~$28–30 | ~30x | ~$840–900 |

The **bull case** rests on three simultaneous accelerants: AI infrastructure capex running ahead of even the most aggressive 2026 projections, High-NA system ASPs confirmed publicly above $350 million per unit, and either an easing of China export restrictions or sufficiently robust demand from TSMC, Samsung, and SK Hynix to absorb the revenue gap. Under this scenario ASML exits 2026 at the top of its guided range, management raises the 2030 revenue target to the upper end of €60 billion, and the market re-rates the stock toward its prior peak multiple.

The **base case** assumes guidance midpoint delivery — €38 billion in net sales, 52–53 percent gross margins, High-NA contributing approximately two to three systems per quarter by late 2026, and China stable at roughly 20 percent of revenue. At 40x forward earnings the stock is priced approximately in line with fair value at current levels, implying modest returns from here absent an upward revision cycle.

The **bear case** is more instructive for what it requires to materialize. A sustained pause in AI infrastructure investment — driven by a model capability plateau or a macro-driven cloud capex contraction — combined with expanded China restrictions covering service revenue from the existing DUV installed base and gross margin headwinds from High-NA manufacturing learning-curve costs would compress both earnings and multiples simultaneously. At 30x forward earnings on depressed EPS, the stock could trade below $1,000. The bear case demands two things going wrong at once, which is why it is a tail scenario rather than a base — but it is a fat tail given geopolitical uncertainty.

## Catalysts and Risks

The key re-rating catalysts are sequenced and partially dependent on each other. First, a formal public disclosure of High-NA average selling price confirmation above $350 million per system would immediately validate the gross margin expansion trajectory to 56–60 percent by 2030. Second, validation of the 2030 revenue scenario — either through a formal guidance upgrade or through customer capacity announcements that make the arithmetic obvious — would compress the risk premium embedded in the current forward multiple. Third, any easing of U.S.-Netherlands export restrictions on China service revenue, even at the margins, would relieve the single largest uncertainty overhanging the stock.

The de-rating risks are lower probability but non-negligible. An AI infrastructure pause — assigned perhaps a 15–20 percent probability over the next 24 months given the concentration of AI capex among a handful of hyperscalers — would reduce EUV order intake below current backlog replacement rates and trigger a bookings-driven selloff reminiscent of the October 2024 dislocation. Extension of China restrictions to cover spare parts or software upgrades for the existing DUV installed base carries perhaps a 10–15 percent probability given the current trajectory of U.S. export control policy; this would directly erode the installed-base management segment that has thus far been insulated from the restrictions. A credible competitive EUV entrant — Nikon has never fully abandoned its research program — remains a 5–10 percent probability over a 10-year horizon, though the manufacturing lead time and supply chain depth ASML has accumulated makes near-term disruption implausible.

The paradox of pricing a monopoly is that the multiple is simultaneously the best evidence for the thesis and the primary source of vulnerability. At 40x forward earnings, ASML has no room for strategic drift, execution shortfalls, or demand surprises — it is priced for a world in which every chip ever manufactured at leading edge passes through a machine built in Veldhoven, forever. History suggests that forecast has been correct. The question is whether, at $1,600 per share, the market has already been paid for knowing it.

chapters.title: The Quarterly Record: Revenue Cadence, Booking Cycles, and Management Commentary
chapters.body:
## The Distortion Year: 2024's China Pull-Forward

The twelve months spanning 2024 presented a deceptive picture of ASML's underlying demand health. Total net sales of approximately €28.3 billion represented a modest increase over 2023's €27.6 billion — but the composition masked a structural distortion. Chinese semiconductor manufacturers, racing to secure DUV immersion tool inventory ahead of progressive U.S. export-control tightening, had pulled forward orders through late 2023 and into the first half of 2024. China's share of net system sales swelled to approximately 36 percent for the full year, a historically anomalous proportion that front-loaded DUV revenue while suppressing the forward order signal. Meanwhile, memory customers in Korea and the United States were digesting excess DRAM and NAND capacity accumulated during the post-pandemic capex surge, damping near-term EUV demand from Samsung and SK Hynix.

The divergence between reported revenue and forward-looking order health became visible — spectacularly, and involuntarily — on October 15, 2024. In what became one of the most consequential clerical errors in semiconductor industry history, ASML's investor relations platform inadvertently published its Q3 2024 financial results approximately twelve hours before the intended release window. The prematurely disclosed figures showed net bookings of €2.6 billion for the quarter — a result that fell sharply below the sell-side consensus range of approximately €5 to €5.5 billion. By the time Amsterdam trading opened, ASML shares had fallen more than 16 percent, erasing roughly €45 billion in market capitalisation in a single session. The accidental release transformed what would have been an ordinary earnings morning into a repricing event: analysts who had modelled China DUV normalisation as a gradual fade were confronted with evidence that the pull-forward had already unwound, and that the AI-driven EUV recovery had not yet arrived in the order book. Full-year 2024 net bookings remained depressed relative to the levels that had sustained the 2022–2023 supercycle, and gross margins compressed as the mix shifted toward lower-margin DUV and away from EUV systems.

## The Recovery Sequence: 2025's AI Inflection

The recovery arrived on schedule — and then accelerated. ASML entered 2025 with guidance that reflected genuine uncertainty about the pace of AI-driven capex commitment from TSMC, Samsung, and SK Hynix. Each successive quarter narrowed that uncertainty in the company's favour.

Full-year 2025 net sales reached €32.7 billion, a 15.5 percent increase over 2024 and a new revenue record, supported by 48 EUV system shipments generating €11.6 billion in EUV revenue — a 39 percent year-on-year increase. The installed-base management segment contributed €8.2 billion, growing faster than the systems business and cementing its role as the margin-stabilising floor of the earnings model. Gross margin for the full year reached 52.8 percent, up from approximately 51.3 percent in 2024, as EUV mix improved and China-related DUV stepped back. Net income was €9.6 billion at a net margin of approximately 29 percent; earnings per share (basic) reached €24.73.

The most significant demand confirmation arrived in Q4 2025. Net bookings for the quarter reached €13.158 billion — the highest single-quarter order intake in ASML's history — of which €7.4 billion was EUV. The figure confirmed that customers were making multi-year capacity commitments driven by AI infrastructure build-out rather than short-cycle restocking. Fouquet, in commentary accompanying the Q4 2025 and full-year 2025 results, described the demand environment as producing "another record year" and noted that customers had exhibited "notably more positive assessments of the medium-term market" as the year progressed. ASML closed 2025 with a record backlog of €38.797 billion — the product of €28.035 billion in full-year net bookings — equivalent to roughly twelve months of forward revenue at the midpoint of the 2026 guidance range and providing a degree of earnings visibility unusual for a capital equipment manufacturer at this point in a recovery cycle.

## Q1 2026: The Benchmark Quarter

| Metric | Q1 2026 |
|---|---|
| Net sales | €8.8 billion |
| Net system sales | €6.3 billion |
| EUV system sales (incl. 2 High-NA) | €4.1 billion+ |
| Installed-base management | €2.5 billion |
| Gross margin | 53% |
| Net income | €2.8 billion |
| Diluted EPS | €7.15 |

ASML's first-quarter 2026 results, reported in April 2026, delivered a performance that exceeded the upper bound of its own prior guidance and prompted a material revision to the full-year outlook. The €8.8 billion headline figure embedded two EXE:5200 High-NA deliveries — each carrying estimated average selling prices of €300–400 million per unit — marking the first quarter in which High-NA systems registered at meaningful revenue scale. The remainder of EUV revenue reflected continued strong NXE:3800E shipment cadence, enhanced by the Q1 2026 release of the PEP-1E productivity upgrade, which extended tool throughput from 220 to 230 wafers per hour. Installed-base management contributed €2.5 billion, consistent with the structural growth trajectory of the service and upgrade segment. Net income of €2.8 billion at €7.15 diluted EPS implied, on an annualised basis, a trajectory well above the full-year 2025 outcome.

On the Q1 2026 earnings call, Fouquet addressed the durability of AI-related demand directly, noting that the breadth of customer capacity commitments had expanded beyond hyperscale logic into memory — specifically citing HBM-related EUV demand from Korean customers as a source of incremental pull. He characterised the pattern of customer behaviour as indicative of sustained structural investment rather than cyclical restocking, and described the AI infrastructure build-out, data-centre capacity expansion, and sovereign chip initiatives as creating reinforcing rather than substitutable demand vectors. The guidance raise that accompanied the results reflected, in management's framing, conservative assumptions relative to current order visibility.

## Guidance Architecture: From €34–39 Billion to €36–40 Billion

ASML's guidance discipline is formally structured: the company issues a full-year revenue range at the start of each fiscal year and raises or narrows it at each quarterly earnings release as shipment and acceptance visibility improves. For 2026, the initial range of €34–39 billion was issued alongside Q4 2025 results in January 2026, spanning a €5 billion band that management attributed to residual uncertainty around China shipment volumes and the precise timing of High-NA revenue recognition.

Following Q1 2026 results, ASML raised the range to €36–40 billion — a €2 billion upward shift at both ends. The revision reflected faster-than-expected customer acceptance rates, earlier-than-modelled High-NA contributions, and the absence of any incremental China restriction deterioration embedded in the conservative scenario. At the midpoint of €38 billion, the raised guidance implies full-year revenue growth of approximately 16 percent over 2025's €32.7 billion.

## The Booking Signal Question

Beginning with Q2 2025 results, ASML discontinued its practice of quarterly net bookings disclosure, shifting to annual-only order data. The decision removed what had been — as the Q3 2024 episode illustrated with considerable market force — one of the most closely watched short-term demand indicators in the semiconductor equipment sector. Sell-side analysts adapted along two lines: some shifted primary focus to backlog delta analysis, inferring implied quarterly order intake from the spread between reported backlog levels and recognised revenue; others increased reliance on customer capex guidance disclosures and supply-chain channel checks as a substitute signal. Neither approach replicates the precision of a direct bookings figure, and the change has structurally widened the quarterly earnings forecast dispersion that analysts assign to ASML.

The Q4 2025 bookings figure of €13.158 billion — disclosed as part of the annual reporting cycle — provided retrospective reassurance that AI demand was translating into binding commitments. The EUV component of €7.4 billion indicated that the mix of new orders was tilted toward leading-edge capacity expansion rather than mature-node replenishment, consistent with the AI logic and HBM demand thesis management had been articulating through 2025.

## Consensus and the Q2 2026 Outlook

ASML guided Q2 2026 net sales to €8.4–9.0 billion at gross margins of 51–52 percent — a slight sequential compression from Q1's 53 percent, reflecting manufacturing cost headwinds as the High-NA production ramp climbs the learning curve and normal quarterly revenue mix variation. The guidance midpoint of €8.7 billion would represent a ninth consecutive quarter of year-on-year revenue growth if achieved, extending the recovery arc that began in early 2025.

Sell-side consensus for full-year 2026 as of the frozen snapshot date coalesces around net sales of approximately €38–39 billion — the upper end of ASML's own guidance range — and diluted earnings per share of approximately €28–32, a spread that captures divergent analyst assumptions across three principal variables: whether further China restrictions materialise before year-end and how aggressively ASML's guidance band accommodates that risk; whether a third EXE:5200 High-NA system can be recognised in fiscal 2026; and the pace of installed-base management growth as the EUV fleet matures and upgrade cycle revenue accumulates. On any scenario consistent with the guidance midpoint, 2026 will mark ASML's second consecutive record revenue year and its first in which High-NA EUV transitions from a research-tool curiosity into a material earnings contributor.

chapters.title: The Board of Management: Fouquet's EUV Pedigree, Dassen's Financial Architecture, and the Post-Wennink Leadership Compact
chapters.body:
## The End of the Founding Generation

On April 24, 2024, ASML's Annual General Meeting in Veldhoven ratified a succession that had been years in the making and months in formal preparation — but that nonetheless marked the end of an era with few equivalents in the history of technology companies. Peter Wennink, who had served as chief financial officer before becoming chief executive in 2013, stepped down after more than three decades at the company. Martin van den Brink, who had joined ASML in 1984 as one of its earliest engineers and had served as president and chief technology officer, departed the same day. Together, the two men had shepherded EUV lithography from a research curiosity into the most valuable monopoly in the global semiconductor supply chain. Their simultaneous exit was not dysfunction — it was a coordinated handover planned with the methodical precision the company applies to its optical alignments.

The departure of Wennink and van den Brink represented something more consequential than a routine CEO transition. They were, in the truest sense, the architects of ASML's moat. Wennink had managed the decades-long EUV investment case to a skeptical investment community, sustaining capital allocation toward a program that consumed billions of euros before a single commercial system shipped. Van den Brink had been the technical soul of the enterprise, co-designing the EUV program's core physics and engineering architecture from its origins in the late 1990s through its commercial debut in 2018 and the subsequent low-NA ramp. What passed to their successors was not merely a set of organizational responsibilities but the stewardship of the most complex and irreplaceable machine humanity has ever manufactured at commercial scale.

## Christophe Fouquet: The Commercialization CEO

Christophe Fouquet was born in France in 1973 and trained as a physicist, earning a master's degree from the Institut National Polytechnique de Grenoble in 1997. His early career traced the contours of the semiconductor equipment industry at its most competitive: stints at Applied Materials as a global product manager and at KLA-Tencor in marketing gave him a landscape view of the tools ecosystem that few career ASML insiders could claim. The competitive intelligence those years accumulated — understanding how process control and deposition companies think about the chip fabrication value chain — would prove durable when Fouquet later found himself negotiating EUV qualification with the world's largest foundries.

He [joined ASML in 2008](https://www.asml.com/en/news/stories/2024/christophe-fouquet-asml-ceo), entering through marketing and product management for EUV at a moment when the program was still pre-commercial and widely doubted outside the company. Over the following decade, he rose through EUV product management, learning the technology's yield characteristics, its customer integration challenges, and the pricing architecture that would determine whether EUV's economics justified the foundry investment required to adopt it. In 2018, the year ASML shipped its first commercial EUV system, Fouquet joined the Board of Management as Executive Vice President of EUV — the role that made him personally responsible for commercializing the product that now defines the company.

That role put Fouquet at the table for the most consequential customer qualification conversations in ASML's history. The decisions made between 2018 and 2022 about EUV pricing, throughput guarantees, and uptime commitments at TSMC, Samsung, and Intel shaped the terms on which the leading-edge semiconductor industry adopted the technology. Fouquet was the company's face in those negotiations. When High-NA EUV now requires analogous qualification conversations — at average selling prices estimated between €300 and €400 million per system, roughly double the low-NA NXE:3800E — the CEO leading that ramp carries firsthand knowledge of how those relationships were built. This is not incidental continuity. It is the strategic logic of his elevation.

Fouquet was promoted to Chief Business Officer in 2022 and assumed the presidency and chief executive role on April 25, 2024. His public communications have consistently emphasized structural demand over cyclical caution. Following first-quarter 2026 results — which showed €8.8 billion in net sales, a 53 percent gross margin, and prompted a full-year guidance raise to €36–40 billion — Fouquet characterized the demand environment as driven by customers "accelerating their capacity buildouts in response to surging AI chip demand," framing the signal as durable rather than cyclical. The distinction matters to investors because the €44–60 billion 2030 revenue scenario requires that AI infrastructure investment sustain elevated semiconductor capex for the better part of a decade. Fouquet has been consistently deliberate in declining to frame the current cycle as a temporary inventory restocking.

## Roger Dassen: Capital Discipline at Scale

CFO Roger Dassen's biography describes a different kind of ASML career — one that arrived not through the engineering pipeline but through the boardroom audit committee. Born in the Netherlands in 1965, Dassen completed a PhD in business and economics at Maastricht University in 1995 and built his career at Deloitte Touche Tohmatsu, where he eventually led the firm's global Technology, Media and Telecom practice. He [joined ASML in 2018](https://www.asml.com/en/company/governance/board-of-management), the same year Fouquet joined the Board of Management.

Where Wennink had managed the EUV investment case to analysts largely on conviction and technical credibility, Dassen brought institutional rigor to a company that had, by 2018, begun generating the free cash flow its decades of patient investment had been targeting. The capital allocation choices under his tenure have been substantial. In 2025, ASML returned approximately €8.5 billion to shareholders through dividends and buybacks while simultaneously spending €4.7 billion on research and development and committing approximately €1.3 billion — roughly $1.5 billion — to Mistral AI as part of a roughly $2 billion fundraising round that made ASML Mistral's largest shareholder and secured a board seat.

The Mistral investment is worth parsing carefully. ASML framed it as strategic: the stated rationale connects to accelerating AI-driven process optimization within ASML's Holistic Lithography software platform and to a broader thesis that European AI sovereignty benefits ASML's long-term operating environment. Whether the return hurdles applied to a venture-stage European AI company are commensurate with those applied to the core R&D allocation is a question Dassen has not answered in detail publicly. What the investment signals is a willingness to deploy balance sheet capital toward strategic optionality at a scale few semiconductor equipment companies would contemplate. The Supervisory Board reappointed Dassen for a new four-year term at the April 2026 AGM, a vote of confidence in the capital allocation framework he has constructed.

## The April 2026 Board Refresh and the CTO Question

The April 2026 Annual General Meeting completed the post-succession restructuring that had been incomplete since van den Brink's departure two years earlier. The Supervisory Board reappointed COO Frédéric Schneider-Maunoury for a two-year term alongside Dassen and formally appointed [Marco Pieters as Chief Technology Officer](https://www.asml.com/en/news/press-releases/2025/asml-appoints-next-chief-technology-officer), expanding the Board of Management to six members.

Schneider-Maunoury remains the least publicly profiled member of the executive team despite overseeing manufacturing and supply chain for a system that contains approximately 100,000 custom parts and takes roughly 18 months to produce. With the High-NA supply chain ramping and an installed base exceeding 5,000 systems globally generating €8.2 billion in annual service revenue, the COO function carries operational consequence that is disproportionate to its investor relations visibility.

The Pieters appointment addresses the structural gap left by van den Brink's departure more directly. A semiconductor industry veteran, Pieters inherits a technology roadmap with clearly defined waypoints — High-NA EUV production ramp through the EXE:5200 platform, Hyper-NA research initiation, and whatever wavelength architecture follows — but inherits it at a moment when the company's founding technologist is no longer present to adjudicate the hardest physics tradeoffs. Whether Pieters' background provides adequate depth to shepherd these transitions through volume production without the institutional authority van den Brink commanded remains the most consequential unanswered question in ASML's leadership structure.

## Supervisory Board Independence

ASML's Supervisory Board provides the oversight layer above the Board of Management. The founding parents — Philips and ASM International — divested their stakes entirely decades ago. The 2012 co-investment arrangement in which Intel, Samsung, and TSMC acquired equity stakes totaling approximately 23 percent as part of the EUV development co-funding arrangement has since unwound: all three customer-shareholders sold their positions, eliminating the structural conflict-of-interest dynamic that characterized that period. Today ASML's major shareholders are institutional — Baillie Gifford, Capital Group, Vanguard, BlackRock — with no controlling block and no customer-affiliated directors creating formal governance entanglement in pricing or technology access decisions.

## The Founder's Shadow

The departure of Wennink and van den Brink in a single April morning raised a question that their successors cannot entirely answer through organizational announcements: what happens to institutional knowledge that was never fully codifiable? IP ownership and patent portfolios protect specific inventions, but the judgment about which physics problems to pursue, which customer integration challenges to absorb rather than transfer, and how to maintain supplier relationships built on decades of mutual dependence — these are not assets that transfer in a governance filing. ASML's structural answer is the depth of its engineering organization, which numbers in the tens of thousands and carries the tacit knowledge of EUV development across multiple layers beneath the executive suite. The more honest answer is that the generation now in charge will be tested not by the problems van den Brink solved but by the ones that arise as High-NA moves from qualification into volume and Hyper-NA moves from whiteboard to prototype. Fouquet understands the technology deeply enough to ask the right questions. Whether Pieters and the organization beneath him can answer them without the original architect in the room is the leadership compact ASML's current chapter has yet to demonstrate.

chapters.title: The Customer Ecosystem: Foundry, Logic, Memory, and the China Exposure Unwind
chapters.body:
## Four Customers, Four Mandates

ASML's revenue base is more concentrated than the breadth of its product catalogue suggests. Four customer groupings account for essentially all system sales: leading-edge foundry and logic fabs, advanced DRAM and HBM producers, mature-node and specialty manufacturers, and Chinese state-backed foundries. The relative weight of each has shifted dramatically over the past two years, and the direction of that shift — away from Chinese DUV volume and toward EUV-intensive AI infrastructure — is the most consequential structural change in ASML's business since EUV first entered commercial production.

The leading-edge foundry and logic cohort — anchored by TSMC, Samsung Foundry, and Intel Foundry — represents the highest-value tier. These three customers collectively absorb virtually all EUV system shipments and are the only confirmed recipients of High-NA EUV tools. EUV revenue reached €11.6 billion in full-year 2025, representing 48 systems at average selling prices well above the NXE:3800E's approximately €180 million list price; the arrival of EXE:5200 High-NA systems, estimated at €300–400 million each, will pull average selling prices materially higher as the mix shifts through the decade. The DRAM and HBM segment — principally SK Hynix, Samsung Memory, and Micron — forms the second tier, consuming both EUV for critical patterning layers and high-end DUV immersion for supporting steps. The mature-node cohort, including GlobalFoundries, Tower Semiconductor, and ams-OSRAM, sustains ASML's DUV installed base and service revenue stream but is insulated from export controls. Chinese fabs sit in the fourth category, one that has undergone the most abrupt redefinition of any customer segment in ASML's four-decade history.

## TSMC: The Demand Anchor

No customer relationship in the semiconductor equipment industry rivals TSMC's centrality to ASML's business. TSMC was one of three equity co-investors in ASML's 2012 capital placement — alongside Intel and Samsung — a transaction that gave the foundry both a financial stake in ASML's success and priority access to EUV supply during the critical early ramp. That relationship has compounded across every subsequent node generation. TSMC deployed NXE:3400C and 3400D systems through its N7+ and N5 nodes, the NXE:3600D at N3, and is now qualifying the EXE:5200 High-NA platform in preparation for N2 and, ultimately, A16 and A14 — ASML's sub-2-nanometer frontier.

The strategic centrality of TSMC for ASML extends beyond Taiwan. TSMC's geographic diversification program, driven by customer and government pressure to reduce single-country concentration, is creating demand across three new continents. TSMC Fabs 21 and 22 in Chandler, Arizona — targeting N4 and then N2 production — require full EUV toolsets that ASML must supply and service from its U.S. customer support infrastructure in Hillsboro and Chandler. Japan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (JASM) Phase 1 in Kumamoto produces at 22nm and 28nm with DUV; Phase 2, slated for 6nm production, introduces EUV demand in a new geography. The European Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (ESMC) joint venture in Dresden — a partnership between TSMC, Bosch, Infineon, and NXP — will produce at 28nm and initially relies on DUV but represents a strategic foothold in Europe. For ASML, this geographic dispersal converts a historically Taiwan-concentrated revenue stream into a more distributed, politically resilient demand profile, while simultaneously expanding the installed-base surface that sustains recurring service revenue.

TSMC's capex trajectory functions as the primary leading indicator for ASML EUV orders. When TSMC signals N2 volume ramp acceleration — as it did through 2025 and into 2026, driven by Apple, Nvidia, AMD, and Broadcom AI chip demand — EUV bookings follow with a roughly 12–18 month lag.
