The record year-end 2025 backlog of €38.797 billion, supported by €28.035 billion in full-year net bookings, reflects precisely this dynamic: TSMC and its peers committed capacity expansion capital ahead of anticipated AI accelerator demand that was itself accelerating.

## HBM and the Memory EUV Inflection

The second demand driver that has emerged with unusual force is high-bandwidth memory. HBM's role in AI accelerators — stacked atop logic dies in packages like Nvidia's GB200 NVL72 and AMD's MI400 — has recast SK Hynix and Samsung Memory from DUV-dominant customers into mixed EUV and DUV buyers with accelerating EUV intensity.

Advanced DRAM production at the 1-alpha and 1-beta nodes requires EUV on the most critical patterning layers, where line-edge roughness and overlay error tolerances cannot be met by even the most sophisticated DUV multi-patterning schemes. SK Hynix, as the dominant HBM supplier for AI accelerators — holding approximately 50 percent of HBM market share through its HBM3E supply to Nvidia — has accelerated EUV investment on its DRAM roadmap as HBM4 qualification ramps. Samsung Memory's 1-beta DRAM node similarly incorporates EUV layers, and Micron's CHIPS Act-funded domestic expansion in Boise, Idaho, and Clay, New York, incorporates both EUV and advanced DUV toolsets for its 1-gamma DRAM roadmap.

The incremental EUV demand from HBM is structurally different from logic EUV demand in one important respect: DRAM layers are fewer and more standardized than the dozen-plus EUV passes required for advanced logic nodes. This means each HBM DRAM fab requires fewer EUV machines than a comparable logic fab but benefits from the same high throughput utilization — the NXE:3800E's enhanced throughput of 230 wafers per hour (following the Q1 2026 PEP-1E productivity package) makes it economically viable for DRAM applications that would have been marginal at earlier throughput levels. As Nvidia's Blackwell Ultra and the anticipated Rubin architecture drive continued HBM volume growth through 2026 and beyond, the memory contribution to ASML's EUV order intake is likely to grow as a proportion of total bookings.

## The China Exposure Unwind

No aspect of ASML's customer strategy has attracted more investor scrutiny than its China exposure, and the data reveals a trajectory that management has been largely transparent about. China's share of net system sales reached approximately 36 percent in full-year 2024, a figure that reflected both genuine domestic fab investment and, critically, front-loading of DUV immersion purchases ahead of anticipated export restrictions. ASML had voluntarily ceased shipping NXE EUV systems to Chinese customers before U.S. export regulations formally required it, correctly anticipating the direction of policy. The subsequent tightening of Dutch and U.S. export controls on DUV immersion tools — the most advanced of which, including the TWINSCAN NXT:2100i, are now effectively blocked for Chinese customers — has accelerated the revenue decline.

By Q1 2026, China's share had fallen to approximately 19 percent of net system sales. Management has guided to a normalized 2026 range of approximately 20–25 percent, acknowledging that some residual basic DUV and dry-scanner business continues and that service revenue from the existing Chinese installed base remains largely intact.

| Period | China % of Net System Sales | Primary Driver |
|---|---|---|
| FY 2024 | ~36% | DUV front-loading ahead of controls |
| Q1 2026 | ~19% | Immersion DUV restrictions in effect |
| 2026 Guidance (normalized) | ~20–25% | Residual basic DUV + installed-base service |

The installed-base service dimension carries an underappreciated tail risk. ASML maintains an installed base of more than 5,000 systems globally; a significant portion of Chinese fabs' production capacity rests on ASML DUV tools that were sold under earlier, permissive export control regimes. Service revenue from this base — calibration, replacement optics, scanner upgrades, and software subscriptions — flows through ASML's installed-base management segment, which generated €8.2 billion globally in 2025. If future policy tightening were to restrict ASML from servicing already-installed Chinese tools, the impact would extend beyond system sales into a recurring revenue stream that currently enjoys higher gross margins than the systems business. Management has not publicly quantified the China-specific component of installed-base revenue, but the scenario is explicitly cited in ASML's risk disclosures as a material downside factor. SMIC's and Hua Hong's ability to sustain advanced DUV production at current yields is itself partially dependent on continued ASML service access — a leverage point that regulators have not yet exercised but that remains a live policy option.

## The Revenue Re-Mix and Its Margin Arithmetic

The strategic reframing that ASML and its investors have largely accepted is that lost China DUV revenue is being replaced by higher-margin EUV demand from AI-driven foundry and memory customers. The arithmetic is directionally favorable: a DUV immersion system sells at roughly €50–80 million with gross margins below the corporate average, while an NXE:3800E sells at approximately €180 million at margins above the corporate average, and an EXE:5200 High-NA sells at an estimated €300–400 million at margins that management has indicated will improve as manufacturing yields on the more complex optical system mature.

The substitution effect does carry one structural friction, however. ASML's DUV manufacturing operations — Cymer light sources in San Diego, wafer stage components in Veldhoven, optical columns from ZEISS SMT in Oberkochen — carry fixed overhead scaled to a volume of DUV system shipments that is now declining. Lower DUV throughput creates manufacturing overhead absorption headwinds that are partially obscured by the EUV margin uplift at the consolidated level. Near-term 2026 gross margin guidance of 51–53 percent, slightly below 2025's 52.8 percent, reflects this dynamic: High-NA EUV systems are in early production ramp, their manufacturing costs are still on the learning curve, and DUV volume is contracting faster than fixed-cost structures can adjust.

Over the medium term, ASML's trajectory toward its 2030 gross margin target of 56–60 percent depends on High-NA EUV maturing along its cost curve while DUV fixed costs are absorbed by continued mature-node demand from non-China customers and the growing installed-base service stream. The re-mix is real, the direction is positive, and the timing remains the primary uncertainty.

chapters.title: Monopoly Mechanics: Why Nikon and Canon Failed, What China Is Building, and Whether High-NA Has a Challenger
chapters.body:
## The Last Men Standing in Lithography

No company other than ASML has shipped a production-ready EUV lithography system. That sentence — simple, flat, almost bureaucratic — is among the most consequential facts in the global semiconductor industry. In a market that determines the physical ceiling of what chips humanity can build, ASML holds a monopoly that is not a matter of pricing strategy or market timing. It is, at its core, a matter of physics.

The clearest way to understand ASML's position is to trace the paths taken by its competitors and the points at which those paths ended. Nikon Corporation and Canon Inc. were not peripheral players. Through the 1980s and 1990s, Nikon in particular dominated the global lithography market with stepper and step-and-scan systems, holding market share at times exceeding 50 percent. Canon occupied the second tier. ASML, the upstart joint venture spun out of Philips and ASM International in a converted Eindhoven office building in 1984, was the challenger.

The competitive inversion happened across roughly two decades and was driven primarily by ASML's early bets on 193-nanometer immersion DUV, which it commercialized ahead of its Japanese rivals, and then on EUV — a technology so technically demanding that Nikon and Canon both assessed the investment required and concluded it was prohibitive. By the mid-2010s, neither had a production EUV program. The market share that once belonged to Nikon now belongs to a technology its leadership declined to pursue.

## Why Physics, Not Price, Sealed the Market

The barriers that protect ASML's EUV monopoly are not the conventional kind — regulatory, intellectual-property fences that can be designed around or financial advantages that patient capital can overcome. They are embedded in three interlocking physical realities that took decades to develop and cannot be replicated on any foreseeable timeline.

The first is the light source. Generating 13.5-nanometer extreme ultraviolet light requires a CO₂ laser striking molten tin droplets at a rate of 50,000 droplets per second — a process that produces plasma whose emitted light is then collected and focused by a mirror system. The laser technology required to do this at the power levels needed for semiconductor production was developed and patented by Cymer, a San Diego company ASML acquired in 2013 for approximately $2.5 billion. Cymer's EUV light sources, and the CO₂ laser subsystems supplied by Trumpf GmbH, represent a supplier relationship that any would-be EUV competitor would need to either replicate from scratch or acquire — neither of which is feasible without building a parallel industrial ecosystem over at least a decade.

The second and most structurally impenetrable barrier is the optical column. Every EUV system requires a series of reflective mirrors — not lenses, since no transparent material transmits 13.5-nanometer light — that are polished to tolerances measured in fractions of a nanometer across surfaces roughly the size of a dinner plate. These mirrors are manufactured exclusively by ZEISS Semiconductor Manufacturing Technology (ZEISS SMT), the optical division of Carl Zeiss AG in Oberkochen, Germany. ASML holds approximately 24 percent of ZEISS SMT, a stake it took specifically to anchor this relationship as the EUV program matured. The accumulated manufacturing knowledge required to produce EUV optics at yield — representing roughly 30 years of precision development — has no known alternative supplier anywhere in the world. A competitor that could fund a light source and a wafer stage would still face an optics bottleneck for which there is currently no second source.

The third barrier is the supply chain itself. Each EUV system contains approximately 100,000 components, many of them custom-designed for the specific mechanical, thermal, and vacuum requirements of EUV lithography, and takes roughly 18 months to manufacture. These are not components available from general industrial suppliers. They are produced by a network of specialized vendors — most of them European — whose relationships with ASML were built incrementally over decades of shared development. The capital investment, IP accumulation, and organizational learning embedded in this supply chain represents a barrier that cannot be surmounted by any combination of capital injection that a realistic competitor could deploy in the timeframe relevant to ASML's 2030 revenue horizon.

## Nikon's Remaining Position and the NIL Wildcard

Nikon did not vanish from lithography after ceding the EUV contest. It retains a meaningful share of the DUV immersion market — the ArF immersion tools used for multi-patterning at nodes between 65nm and approximately 20nm — where it competes with ASML's TWINSCAN NXT:2100i and NXT:2050i platforms. Nikon's market share in immersion DUV is materially smaller than ASML's, but the installed base and ongoing service relationships are real.

More interesting, and more frequently cited as a competitive variable, is Nikon's development of nanoimprint lithography (NIL). NIL is a contact-based patterning technique in which a template physically stamps a pattern into a photoresist rather than optically projecting it, enabling extremely fine feature resolution at lower cost than photolithography. Nikon has partnered with Canon (which has its own NIL program under the FPA brand) and semiconductor customers in the NAND and DRAM spaces to develop NIL for memory applications, where the pattern layouts are highly regular and the contact-stamping approach is more viable than in logic.

NIL is real technology and is not being dismissed by the equipment industry. But its application domain is bounded in ways that matter for ASML's competitive position. NIL cannot today produce the overlay accuracy required for advanced logic — the multi-layer alignment tolerances at sub-5nm nodes that ASML's EUV platforms achieve with wafer-stage positioning measured in picometers. Its template wear and throughput characteristics also limit its applicability in high-volume production contexts. For DRAM and NAND, where the pitch scaling targets are less aggressive than in leading-edge logic, NIL may capture a portion of new tool spending that would otherwise go to DUV multi-patterning schemes. This is not irrelevant — DRAM represents a meaningful component of ASML's DUV revenue — but NIL in memory does not challenge ASML's EUV franchise or its high-end immersion DUV business. The competitive perimeter is narrow and the probability of it widening to threaten ASML's core economics before 2030 is low.

## China's Long March Toward 28nm

The more geopolitically loaded competitive question is not whether Nikon can challenge ASML's EUV monopoly, but whether China can build one. The answer requires separating what China has demonstrably achieved from what it has announced as aspiration.

Shanghai Micro Electronics Equipment Group (SMEE) is China's primary domestic lithography developer. SMEE has produced working DUV systems capable of exposing features at 90-nanometer resolution — a tool comparable to equipment ASML was shipping in the early 2000s. Reports through 2025 indicated SMEE was targeting 28nm immersion capability, which would bring it to the threshold of what ASML's current immersion tools begin at. The technical gap between SMEE's demonstrated 90nm capability and ASML's TWINSCAN NXT:2100i — which operates at below 10nm in multi-patterning configurations and supports production at nodes critical to advanced DRAM and mature logic — is not measured in generations. It is measured in approximately two decades of commercial development.

| Capability | SMEE (current) | ASML NXT:2100i |
|---|---|---|
| Demonstrated resolution | ~90nm | <10nm (multi-patterning) |
| Immersion production | Not confirmed | Full production |
| Overlay accuracy | Undisclosed | <1.5nm machine-to-machine |
| Throughput (wph) | Undisclosed | ~295 wph |

The timeline to 28nm immersion from 90nm dry is not a linear extension of existing capability. It requires a light source at 193nm with the coherence and power stability needed for immersion, a lens column with the numerical aperture and aberration control required for production-worthy overlay, and a wafer stage with sub-nanometer positioning under full thermal and vibrational loading. SMEE must also build a supply chain for the components it cannot manufacture domestically — a task complicated by the same export controls that are reducing ASML's China revenue, since optical components and precision mechanical subsystems are also subject to restriction.

The strategic relevance to ASML is further modulated by the geography of the threat. China's export-control exposure has already reduced ASML's China share from approximately 36 percent of net system sales in 2024 to roughly 19 percent in Q1 2026. The Chinese customers most affected by export restrictions — SMIC, Hua Hong, and their affiliates — are the same customers that would, in theory, purchase domestic SMEE tools as a substitute. ASML has already largely priced out advanced China shipments. Lost China DUV revenue is being structurally replaced by higher-margin EUV demand from AI-driven customers in Taiwan, Korea, and the United States — a mix shift that is widening gross margins even as the absolute China exposure declines.

## The Installed-Base Moat Nobody Discusses

Competitive analysis of ASML tends to focus on new tool sales, where the EUV monopoly is most visible. It less frequently addresses the competitive advantage embedded in the installed base of more than 5,000 systems deployed globally across every major semiconductor manufacturer — a base that generates a parallel and increasingly dominant revenue stream.

Installed-base management — comprising scanner upgrades, optical column improvements, service contracts, and Holistic Lithography software subscriptions — contributed €8.2 billion in 2025, representing approximately 25 percent of total revenue and the fastest-growing and most margin-resilient segment of the business. Service revenue of this scale, generated from systems with 10-to-20-year operational lifespans, creates a recurring income floor that persists through capex down cycles. No challenger entering the lithography market — even one that could eventually produce a competitive tool — would inherit any portion of this installed-base economics. They would begin at zero service revenue against ASML's compounding recurring stream.

## The Probability of a Challenger

What would it take for a competitor to challenge ASML's EUV monopoly by 2030? The honest structural answer is: it would require simultaneous, coordinated mastery of extreme-ultraviolet light source technology, high-precision reflective optics manufacturing, picometer-accuracy wafer-stage engineering, and a 100,000-component custom supply chain — all developed in parallel, to production-yield specifications, in approximately four years. No commercial entity is on a trajectory to accomplish this. No nation-state program has demonstrated the supply chain prerequisites.

The scenario most frequently modeled by analysts is a China-funded EUV program with unlimited capital. Even granting that scenario, the commercialization timeline from a notional first EUV prototype to production-qualified systems at a major foundry is typically a decade or longer — ASML's own EUV program ran from the late 1990s to first commercial shipment in 2018. A Chinese EUV program that achieved a research-scale demonstration by 2030 would not represent a commercial threat to ASML's revenue horizon within that same window. The probability of a credible EUV challenger disrupting ASML's core business by 2030 is, by any realistic appraisal, less than five percent.

The more consequential competitive risk for ASML is not the emergence of a rival but the possibility that AI infrastructure investment pauses, reducing the pull-through demand that is currently accelerating EUV and High-NA adoption. That risk is macroeconomic, not competitive — and ASML's record €38.797 billion order backlog at year-end 2025 provides multi-year insulation against even a meaningful demand interruption.

chapters.title: The News Record and Forward Catalyst Map: From High-NA Seeding to Guidance Raises
chapters.body:
## A Two-Year Timeline of Inflection Points

The twenty-four months between the spring of 2024 and the frozen snapshot date of May 23, 2026, produced more structurally significant news for ASML than any comparable window since the first commercial EUV shipment in 2018. The sequence ran from leadership succession and an embarrassing data leak through record order intake, a landmark strategic investment, and an earnings beat that forced analysts to revise multi-year models upward in a single afternoon.

**April 25, 2024 — The Generational Handover.** Peter Wennink, the CEO who had shepherded ASML through the entire EUV commercialization arc, retired alongside CTO Martin van den Brink, the engineer who had spent decades betting the company on extreme-ultraviolet light. Both roles changed hands simultaneously: Christophe Fouquet assumed the presidency, and the CTO seat was left structurally vacant until the April 2026 AGM filled it with Marco Pieters. The dual departure was ASML's deepest executive transition since its 1995 IPO — and the market's muted reaction reflected confidence in Fouquet, who had personally led EUV commercialization as EVP from 2018 to 2022.

**EXE:5000 Seeding — Three Customers, Five Systems.** Beginning in 2024 and completing in Q1 2025, ASML delivered its first five High-NA EUV tools — the EXE:5000, carrying an estimated average selling price of €300–400 million per unit — to the three foundry and logic customers universally understood to be TSMC, Intel, and Samsung. These were research-phase tools, not production machines; revenue recognition depended on customer acceptance rather than physical delivery. The seeding established the technical foundation that ASML's successor machine, the EXE:5200, would need to productionize. No competitor has shipped a comparable system at any stage of development.

**October 2024 — The Accidental Earnings Release.** In what ASML later described as an inadvertent publication error, its Q3 2024 results reached the market roughly twelve hours before the scheduled announcement. The numbers themselves were the shock: order intake came in sharply below analyst consensus, driven by weakened near-term memory capex and early signs of Chinese customers front-loading DUV purchases ahead of anticipated export restrictions. The stock fell approximately 16 percent on the day of the leak and declined roughly 30 percent from its 2024 peak in the weeks that followed — one of the sharpest single-quarter re-ratings in ASML's listed history. The episode also exposed the degree to which ASML's quarterly order disclosure had become a closely tracked short-term demand signal; management subsequently discontinued quarterly booking disclosures beginning in Q2 2025, shifting to annual-only data.

**Full-Year 2024 — A Year of Transition.** China's share of net system sales reached approximately 36 percent in 2024 as local customers accelerated DUV purchases in anticipation of tightening export controls. It was a pull-forward rather than a structural demand increase, and investors who understood the mechanics were already discounting a sharp China revenue decline in 2025 and 2026.

**Full-Year 2025 — Record Revenue, Record Backlog.** By year-end 2025, the narrative had shifted decisively. ASML reported net sales of €32.7 billion — a 15.5 percent increase over 2024 — with net income of €9.6 billion at a 52.8 percent gross margin. EUV system sales reached €11.6 billion on 48 systems shipped, a 39 percent increase in units over the prior year. The installed-base management segment generated €8.2 billion, representing roughly 25 percent of total revenue and growing structurally faster than the systems business. The year-end backlog of [€38.797 billion](https://www.asml.com/en/news/press-releases/2026/q4-2025-financial-results) — of which Q4 2025 bookings alone contributed €13.158 billion, including €7.4 billion of EUV — provided multi-year forward visibility that no peer in the semiconductor equipment sector could match.

**2025 — The Mistral AI Investment.** Against the backdrop of record operating cash flows, ASML committed approximately €1.3 billion to Mistral AI's approximately $2 billion fundraising round, becoming the French AI laboratory's largest shareholder and securing a board seat. The strategic rationale invoked AI-driven process optimization within ASML's Holistic Lithography platform, but the investment also carried an explicitly geopolitical dimension: ASML framed European AI sovereignty as a long-term commercial interest for a company whose machines define the physical frontier of global chip production.

**Q1 2026 — The Guidance Raise.** First-quarter 2026 results delivered €8.8 billion in net sales at a 53 percent gross margin and €2.8 billion in net income. Two High-NA EXE:5200 systems contributed to over €4.1 billion of EUV revenue in the quarter — an early signal that High-NA volume was beginning to inflect. Management raised full-year 2026 net sales guidance to €36–40 billion from the prior €34–39 billion range, citing "customers accelerating their capacity buildouts in response to surging AI chip demand." The stock's 118 percent appreciation in the twelve months through May 2026 partially recouped the Q3 2024 dislocation.

**April 2026 AGM — The Board Refresh.** At the annual general meeting, the Supervisory Board reappointed CFO Roger Dassen for a new four-year term, extended COO Frédéric Schneider-Maunoury's mandate by two years, and appointed Marco Pieters as Chief Technology Officer — filling the vacancy left by Van den Brink's retirement twenty-four months earlier. The Board of Management expanded to six members, signaling institutional depth in a succession cycle that had run for two years on deliberate continuity rather than transformational disruption.

## The Forward Catalyst Map: 2026–2027

| Catalyst | Timing | Bull Case Impact | Bear Case Impact |
|---|---|---|---|
| EXE:5200 customer acceptance at TSMC N2 | Q2–Q4 2026 | Revenue recognition pulls into 2026; guidance raised again | Delays push revenue into 2027; guidance range widens |
| EXE:5400 / Hyper-NA specification announcement | 2026–2027 | Demonstrates roadmap depth; extends monopoly horizon | Silence raises investor questions on post-High-NA timeline |
| TSMC Arizona fab EUV tooling orders | 2026–2027 | Geopolitically insulated demand; reduces Taiwan concentration risk | Permitting or CHIPS Act funding delays push orders right |
| Q2/Q3 2026 earnings — guidance narrowing | Q3–Q4 2026 | Convergence toward €40B top end; re-rates multiples upward | Miss or warning tightens toward €36B floor; cycle concerns return |
| U.S. export rules on China DUV service revenue | Ongoing | No escalation — €8.2B installed-base business unaffected | Service restrictions expand; removes ASML's most durable China revenue stream |

The single most consequential near-term catalyst is EXE:5200 customer acceptance timing. High-NA systems at ASML's estimated €300–400 million ASP carry gross margin characteristics that are, by management's own framing, temporarily dilutive during production ramp — meaning that the faster acceptance comes, the faster ASML climbs the learning curve toward the 56–60 percent gross margin target embedded in the 2030 scenario.

## The Geopolitical Binary: Trade Relief vs. Service Restriction

China's export control trajectory presents the most asymmetric swing factor in ASML's forward estimates. The base case — already embedded in 2026 guidance — assumes continued restriction of advanced DUV immersion shipments with China contributing roughly 15–20 percent of net system sales, down from 36 percent in 2024.

The upside surprise is a U.S.–China trade agreement that softens export licensing criteria and permits ASML to resume certain immersion tool shipments. Given the structural role DUV plays in Chinese domestic chip production, even a partial relaxation could add €2–4 billion of annualized system revenue at minimal incremental cost — a positive earnings surprise with no R&D or capex requirement.

The downside surprise is categorically more severe: expanded U.S. controls that extend restrictions beyond new system shipments to cover service contracts, spare parts, and software updates for the existing China installed base. ASML's installed-base management segment generated €8.2 billion globally in 2025; a meaningful fraction of that revenue derives from service obligations on the several hundred DUV tools already deployed at SMIC, Hua Hong, and affiliated Chinese fabs. Restrictions on service revenue would threaten the most recurring, highest-margin component of ASML's China exposure — and unlike system-sale restrictions, which affect only future shipments, service restrictions could impair revenue from assets already on customers' floors.

## The Mistral AI Wildcard

The €1.3 billion Mistral AI position deserves separate treatment in any forward catalyst framework, because it introduces a financial asset with optionality characteristics that are alien to ASML's normal industrial earnings model. Mistral AI is a private company; the investment sits on ASML's balance sheet at cost or fair value until a liquidity event — most likely a public listing — forces mark-to-market recognition.

If Mistral AI achieves commercial scale and proceeds to an IPO at a valuation that rewards early investors, ASML's unrealized gain could be substantial — potentially adding billions of euros to book value in a single reporting period. The accounting treatment would flow through other comprehensive income or a revaluation gain depending on how the stake is classified. For investors sizing ASML's intrinsic value, it is worth separating the strategic rationale (AI process optimization) from the financial optionality: even if the operational synergies never fully materialize, a successful Mistral IPO could generate a one-time gain equivalent to several quarters of net income. Conversely, if Mistral AI fails to achieve commercial traction in a crowded AI model market, the write-down risk on a €1.3 billion position is meaningful in absolute terms — though modest relative to ASML's €9.6 billion annual net income. The asymmetry is long-skewed: the upside of a well-timed AI unicorn exit exceeds the manageable downside of a partial impairment.

chapters.title: The Intellectual Property Fortress: 38,000 Patents, R&D Architecture, and the Cymer Acquisition Legacy
chapters.body:
## The R&D Engine Behind the Monopoly

The most revealing number in ASML's 2025 annual accounts is not its €32.7 billion in revenue or its 52.8 percent gross margin. It is the €4.7 billion it spent on research and development — approximately 14 percent of net sales, a 14 percent increase year-over-year, and a figure that exceeds the entire R&D budgets of each of its nearest semiconductor equipment peers in absolute terms. That gap is not a quarterly artifact. It is structural, and it explains why ASML's monopoly has proved impervious to every attempt at replication.

| Company | R&D Spend (approx.) | As % of Revenue |
|---|---|---|
| ASML | €4.7B (2025) | ~14% |
| Applied Materials | ~$2.5B | ~7% |
| Lam Research | ~$1.8B | ~8% |
| KLA Corporation | ~$1.1B | ~12% |

The comparison understates the divergence. Applied Materials and Lam Research spread their R&D across etch, deposition, chemical-mechanical planarization, and other process steps. ASML concentrates its spend on a single, irreproducible technology platform. The cumulative R&D investment underlying a modern EUV system stretches back to the late 1990s; the cost of replicating that accumulated knowledge base — assuming a potential entrant could even assemble the necessary talent and supply relationships — is not a number anyone has been willing to spend.

## The Patent Fortress: 38,000 Filings Across 32 Jurisdictions

The IP architecture that ASML has built around its technology platform comprises approximately 38,000 active patents filed across 32 jurisdictions, with the heaviest concentration in the United States and Japan — the home markets of its largest customers and the venues where infringement litigation carries the greatest commercial consequence.

The portfolio does not merely protect end products. It spans the full technology stack: the physics and engineering of EUV light-source generation, the optical column design and manufacturing tolerances required to deliver 13.5-nanometer light with sufficient coherence and intensity, the wafer stage precision mechanics that must position wafers to sub-picometer accuracy during exposure, the reticle handling and mask-blank inspection systems that maintain pattern fidelity, and the Holistic Lithography software platform that integrates source, mask, and scanner data into an optimization loop. Critically, ASML's IP extends into the manufacturing processes and supplier ecosystem itself — covering not just what the machine does but how it must be built and calibrated.

This layering means that a competitor could not simply design around the product patents. It would need to independently develop — and legally establish freedom-to-operate across — every layer of a system that ASML has been patenting continuously for four decades.

## The Cymer Acquisition: Closing the Last Gap

Before 2013, the most significant external vulnerability in ASML's technology stack was not optical — it was light. EUV lithography requires a plasma-based light source that generates 13.5-nanometer radiation at sufficient power and repetition rate to enable commercial throughput. The dominant independent maker of both excimer laser DUV light sources and EUV light-source technology was Cymer, a San Diego-based company that had worked alongside ASML on EUV source development for years.

ASML acquired Cymer in 2013 for approximately $2.5 billion. The transaction was simultaneously a supply-chain integration move — removing the risk that a critical single-source supplier could be acquired by a rival, could fail commercially, or could extract rents from its sole customer — and an IP consolidation. Cymer held fundamental patents on excimer laser design and EUV light-source physics. Bringing those patents in-house closed what had been the most legally and operationally exposed seam in ASML's IP architecture. The San Diego facility today serves as the center of ASML's light-source engineering, and the Cymer IP base underpins every EUV system that has shipped since 2018's first commercial delivery.

## The ZEISS SMT Partnership: Structural Stability or Latent Risk?

ASML's relationship with Carl Zeiss SMT — the optics subsidiary based in Oberkochen, Germany — is the remaining significant external dependency in the EUV supply chain, and it is structured in a way designed to make that dependency permanent rather than transient. ASML co-funds lens development at ZEISS SMT and holds approximately 24 percent equity in the optics business. ZEISS SMT, in turn, develops and manufactures the extreme-precision mirror and optical column systems that are integral to every EUV scanner — components produced nowhere else on earth and requiring surface smoothness tolerances measured in fractions of an atomic radius.

The commercial arrangement is exclusive: ZEISS SMT does not supply EUV optics to any other customer because no other customer manufactures EUV systems. The partnership functions in practice as a quasi-IP joint venture. ZEISS SMT holds the optics IP, but its commercial viability depends entirely on ASML orders; ASML controls the end-market and the system integration. The structure is stable as long as neither party has an incentive to exit — and the economics of the existing arrangement make defection irrational for both sides. The theoretical long-run risk, that ZEISS SMT could license its optics IP to a new entrant, is constrained by the exclusivity of the relationship and the reality that optics alone would not enable a competitor to build a functioning EUV scanner.

## Trade Secrets and the China Incident

ASML's IP fortress has not been entirely immune to breach. In 2023, ASML disclosed that a former employee in China had accessed proprietary source code without authorization; the company subsequently filed suit. The incident crystallized a risk category that patents cannot fully address: trade-secret exposure, particularly in jurisdictions where enforcement is uncertain and geopolitical tensions create adversarial incentives.

ASML responded by accelerating changes to its information security architecture — segmenting access to critical source-technology documentation more aggressively and reducing the surface area of sensitive IP visible to personnel in higher-risk geographies. The episode also reinforced ASML management's support for export control regimes that limit the transfer of not just hardware but process knowledge to certain customers. In an era when the full value of ASML's franchise rests not merely on the physical machines it ships but on the accumulated engineering knowledge embedded in how those machines are designed, built, and optimized, protecting that knowledge has become as strategically significant as protecting the patent portfolio itself.

chapters.title: Six Risks That Could Break the Monopoly Premium
chapters.body:
## The Six Fault Lines

ASML's monopoly architecture is genuinely formidable. No competitor manufactures a production EUV system. The backlog at the end of 2025 stood at €38.797 billion. The 2030 revenue scenario stretches to €60 billion. Yet the premium attached to that architecture — a forward price-to-earnings multiple of approximately 40x — prices in near-flawless execution across a decade that contains several distinct categories of risk. Six of those risks deserve close examination, because any one of them, if it materialises, could impair shareholder returns even as the monopoly itself survives intact.

---

## Risk 1: China Export Control Escalation

China contributed approximately 36 percent of ASML's net system sales in full-year 2024, nearly all of it from DUV immersion and dry tools. By Q1 2026, progressive U.S. export restrictions had reduced that share to roughly 19 percent, and ASML's 2026 guidance bandwidth of €36–40 billion was explicitly engineered to absorb further China uncertainty. The market has largely priced the DUV system loss. What it has not priced is the next regulatory lever.

The installed-base management segment — service contracts, optical column upgrades, spare parts, and Holistic Lithography software subscriptions — generated €8.2 billion across ASML's global installed base in 2025. A meaningful fraction of that revenue derives from the approximately 500-plus DUV systems already operating inside Chinese fabs, tools that were delivered legally and remain in production. Under current rules, service and spare-parts revenue for the existing China installed base is not subject to export controls. That is precisely what makes it the obvious next target in any escalation scenario.

If U.S. policymakers extended controls to cover service and spare parts for the China installed base — a measure that would effectively degrade Chinese fab productivity over time as systems fall into disrepair — ASML's exposure could be material. Even a conservative estimate of 10–15 percent of installed-base revenue originating from Chinese systems implies €820 million to €1.2 billion of annual recurring revenue at risk. In a more aggressive scenario involving full servicing prohibition, China's existing DUV fabs would face progressive yield degradation and throughput decline, creating second-order demand destruction for Chinese semiconductor output but first-order revenue risk for ASML's highest-margin segment.

The geopolitical trajectory as of the frozen snapshot suggested escalation remained more likely than stabilisation. ASML disclosed no formal breakout of China service revenue in its public filings, making precise quantification difficult — itself a disclosure gap that analysts highlighted as a source of residual uncertainty in the bull case.

---

## Risk 2: AI Capex Pause or Digestion

ASML's raised 2026 guidance was explicitly predicated on AI infrastructure investment. CEO Christophe Fouquet, in the Q1 2026 earnings call, attributed the upgrade to customers "accelerating their capacity buildouts in response to surging AI chip demand." That attribution is both the thesis and the vulnerability.

The semiconductor equipment industry has experienced at least one severe capex digestion cycle in living memory: the 2022–2023 memory inventory correction, during which DRAM and NAND capex collapsed by more than 40 percent and equipment order intake fell sharply across the sector. ASML was not immune — 2024 revenues stepped down from the 2023 peak as memory customers deferred orders. The EUV monopoly does not insulate ASML from capex cycle timing; it merely elevates the baseline around which the cycle oscillates.

A 12–18 month pause in AI semiconductor capex — analogous to, but potentially shallower than, the 2022–2023 memory correction — would produce identifiable damage across three financial dimensions. Order intake, which ASML shifted to annual-only disclosure beginning in Q2 2025, would decline sharply against a 2025 baseline that included €28.035 billion in full-year net bookings. Backlog drawdown would continue at the contracted pace, providing revenue support for roughly 12 months at the midpoint of 2026 guidance, but the post-backlog revenue profile would compress. Gross margin improvement would stall, because the path from 52–53 percent to the 56–60 percent 2030 target requires High-NA mix to increase — and High-NA volumes depend on the same AI-driven capex impulse that funds TSMC's N2 and Samsung's 2nm ramp.

The key diagnostic is whether AI semiconductor demand follows the historical memory inventory cycle or whether the structural pull from hyperscaler capex is sufficiently durable and diversified to compress the digestion phase. Fouquet described customers exhibiting "notably more positive assessments of the medium-term market" by the end of 2025, but management commentary on capex durability at the peak of a cycle is structurally optimistic.

---

## Risk 3: High-NA Adoption Delay

High-NA EUV is ASML's primary ASP expansion vehicle. The EXE:5200, which succeeded the five seeding-phase EXE:5000 units, carries estimated average selling prices of €300–400 million per system, roughly double the NXE:3800E's approximately €180 million list price. ASML's path from 52–53 percent gross margins toward the 56–60 percent 2030 target depends substantially on High-NA mix increasing over the next four years.

The technology is at Phase 1 — research — with three customers, understood to be TSMC, Intel, and Samsung. Pilot production (Phase 2) is expected in 2026–2027; volume production on critical device layers (Phase 3) lies beyond 2027. The transition from research to volume involves qualification challenges that have historically proven difficult to predict: resist chemistry for the 0.55 NA system requires new photoresist formulations with adequate sensitivity and resolution at lower EUV doses; throughput ramp from initial acceptance rates toward the 180-plus wafers per hour needed for economic production involves tuning scanner uptime, reticle handling, and environmental control; and defectivity — the rate of pattern defects per wafer that compromises yield — must reach sub-parts-per-billion levels before customers commit critical-layer production.

If Phase 2 qualification slips by 12–18 months due to any of these factors, ASML's ASP expansion thesis is deferred by a corresponding interval, and the gross margin improvement trajectory must be funded through a longer period of low-NA EUV productivity enhancements like the NXE:3800E PEP-1E package that raised throughput from 220 to 230 wafers per hour in Q1 2026 — incremental rather than transformational margin improvement.

---

## Risk 4: Valuation Compression Without an Earnings Miss

At approximately 40x forward earnings and an EV/Sales ratio of approximately 15.7x as of May 2026, ASML's valuation embeds both the monopoly premium and a secular growth narrative. A stock priced at those multiples carries meaningful exposure to multiple compression even in the absence of an operational miss.

The mechanism is straightforward. If the broad technology sector undergoes a re-rating — driven by rising real interest rates, a generative AI commercialisation disappointment, or a shift in institutional capital allocation away from long-duration growth assets — ASML's forward P/E could compress from 40x toward the low 30s, representing a 20–25 percent decline in share price even if earnings per share continue to grow. The stock's own five-year P/E band, centred around 35–45x before the 2024 post-earnings dislocation, suggests that 40x is not historically extreme but is toward the upper end of the sustainable range in a normalised interest-rate environment. Free cash flow yield of approximately 1.6 percent at May 2026 prices provides minimal cushion against a sentiment shift.

---

## Risk 5: Geopolitical Supply Chain Disruption

ASML's system assembly depends on a concentrated and largely European supply chain that has no redundant parallel. ZEISS SMT in Oberkochen, Germany, manufactures the optical columns — the mirror assemblies and projection optics — that are physically unique to each EUV generation. Trumpf in Ditzingen, Germany, supplies the CO₂ laser systems that drive the tin-droplet light source. Additional specialised suppliers are distributed across the Netherlands, Belgium, and the United Kingdom.

A disruption scenario — whether a European-level sanctions regime on Dutch technology exports, a conflict scenario affecting German industrial suppliers, or a severe logistics breakdown — would halt EUV system deliveries with no viable short-term substitute. Unlike consumer electronics supply chains, ASML cannot reroute component sourcing because the components themselves are manufactured to tolerances that no alternative supplier currently meets. The 18-month manufacturing cycle for an EUV system means that disruption of even a single critical subsystem would propagate through to customer delivery timelines many quarters later.

---

## Risk 6: Key Person and Technology Succession

The simultaneous retirement in April 2024 of CEO Peter Wennink — ASML's chief commercial architect and the executive who stewarded the decade-long EUV investment case to commercialisation — and CTO Martin van den Brink, who had co-led the EUV programme from its origins in the late 1990s, removed the two longest-tenured institutors of ASML's defining technology in a single transition event. Van den Brink was not merely a manager of EUV development; he was one of its inventors. His mental model of the ZEISS SMT partnership, the physics of the tin-droplet plasma source, and the optical design choices underlying both low-NA and High-NA systems represented institutional knowledge that is not fully documentable in engineering specifications.

Marco Pieters was appointed CTO only at the April 2026 AGM — a gap of two years from van den Brink's departure during which the CTO function was managed through existing senior technical staff. Pieters brings semiconductor industry credentials, but the specifics of his prior EUV system architecture involvement are less publicly established than those of his predecessor, and the High-NA programme — which introduces an anamorphic optical design, a new reticle format, and an entirely distinct process integration challenge — is precisely the moment at which CTO continuity matters most.

ASML's principal organisational mitigant is the depth of its technical staff: the company employs more than 44,000 people, with a substantial engineering core that participated in EUV development through multiple product generations. The ZEISS SMT relationship is institutionally maintained through longstanding engineering and commercial teams on both sides. But the simultaneous loss of the two executives who built the culture of that partnership, in the same quarter, is a succession risk that the market has largely dismissed given Fouquet's product-native credentials — and that deserves continued monitoring as High-NA enters the technically demanding transition from research to pilot production.

chapters.title: The Next Twelve Months: Catalysts, Milestones, and the Data Points That Define the Bull/Bear Setup
chapters.body:
## The Catalyst Calendar: Q2 2026 Through Q1 2027

ASML enters the next twelve months from a position of unusual clarity. The company holds roughly €38 billion in order backlog — approximately a full year of revenue at the raised 2026 guidance midpoint — and the Q1 2026 print of €8.8 billion at 53 percent gross margin ran above the sequential Q4 2025 level and above what most analysts had modeled. The question is not whether ASML's business is strong; it plainly is. The question is whether the next four earnings events can sustain a valuation that already prices in a great deal of the good news.

ASML reports quarterly results on a Tuesday approximately three weeks after quarter-end, placing the next four events at roughly July 21 for Q2 2026, October 20 for Q3 2026, January 20, 2027 for Q4 and full-year 2026, and April 21, 2027 for Q1 2027. ASML discontinued quarterly order-intake disclosure beginning Q2 2025 — a decision that removed the single most closely watched near-term demand indicator and increased forecast uncertainty. In its absence, investors must infer the quarterly order run-rate from the delta between reported backlog and revenue recognized. Any material, sustained decline in that implied figure would indicate booking momentum has slipped below the recognition rate.

| Quarter | Est. Earnings Date | Consensus Net Sales | Gross Margin | Key Operational Milestone | Geopolitical Watchpoint |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q2 2026 | ~Jul 21, 2026 | €8.4–9.0B (co. guidance) | 51–52% (co. guidance) | First EXE:5200 conditional acceptances; NXE:3800E PEP-1E volume shipments | U.S. BIS review of DUV service-license scope |
| Q3 2026 | ~Oct 20, 2026 | ~€9.5–10.0B | ~52% | EXE:5200 pilot-production acceptance revenue; TSMC Arizona first-tool commissioning | Dutch government export-permit renewal conditions |
| Q4 2026 | ~Jan 20, 2027 | ~€11.0–11.5B | ~52–53% | Year-end EUV acceptance flush; High-NA 2027 order visibility | CHIPS Act implementation; allied-nation coordination on ASML restrictions |
| Q1 2027 | ~Apr 21, 2027 | ~€9.0–9.5B | ~53% | EXE:5200 volume ramp confirmation; 2027 annual guidance issuance | China service-revenue licensing outcome |

*Q2 2026 net sales guidance of €8.4–9.0 billion and gross margin of 51–52 percent are from ASML's Q1 2026 earnings release. Q3–Q1 2027 estimates are analyst-derived from backlog trajectory and management's raised full-year 2026 guidance of €36–40 billion net sales at 51–53 percent gross margin.*

The Q2 guidance range warrants specific attention. Management guided gross margin to 51–52 percent — a full percentage point below Q1 2026's 53 percent print. The compression reflects High-NA manufacturing cost headwinds: early EXE:5200 units carry above-normal build costs as ASML climbs the production learning curve, and their recognition cadence is lumpy by nature. A Q2 gross margin closer to 52 percent rather than 51 percent would be a constructive signal for the full-year trajectory; a print below 51 percent would reopen debate about High-NA unit economics. Full-year 2026 analyst consensus has coalesced near the €38 billion midpoint of guidance — roughly €29 billion in H2 2026 shared across Q3 and a seasonally strong Q4 — with basic earnings per share expected in the €29–32 range on approximately 385 million shares.

## Seven Data Points That Define Each Quarter

With quarterly bookings off the public record, investors are left with a tighter set of observables. Seven metrics define beat versus miss.

**Gross margin versus guidance midpoint.** Each 50-basis-point beat above the midpoint signals either High-NA cost-curve improvement or favorable EUV service mix. A sustained beat across consecutive quarters would shift the full-year trajectory toward 53 percent and begin to close the gap toward management's 56–60 percent 2030 target.

**EUV revenue as a share of total systems revenue.** In Q1 2026, EUV revenue exceeded €4.1 billion, with two High-NA units contributing materially. As EXE:5200 volumes ramp through the year, the EUV share of total systems revenue should rise. Stagnation would suggest either recognition timing slippage or stronger-than-expected DUV demand from non-restricted markets compensating for slower High-NA acceptance.

**High-NA unit revenue recognized per quarter.** The EXE:5200 carries an estimated average selling price of €300–400 million versus approximately €180 million for the NXE:3800E. Each additional High-NA recognition event adds roughly €200 million of incremental ASP versus a low-NA swap. Any quarter where inferred High-NA unit count exceeds two is a tangible upside signal.

**Installed-base management growth rate.** At €8.2 billion in 2025, installed-base management is ASML's most recurring revenue stream. Growth above 10 percent year-over-year — implying a trajectory toward €9 billion-plus in 2026 — confirms the flywheel of service contracts, optical-column upgrades, and Holistic Lithography software subscriptions that insulates ASML's earnings floor in capex down-cycles.

**Implied quarterly net bookings from backlog delta.** With year-end 2025 backlog at €38.797 billion, and assuming Q1 2026 revenue of €8.8 billion was recognized without full replenishment, backlog entering Q2 likely stood in the €30–32 billion range. The magnitude of that drawdown — and whether subsequent quarters rebuild it — is the primary proxy for order health.

**China revenue as a percentage of net system sales.** China fell from approximately 36 percent of 2024 net system sales to roughly 19 percent in Q1 2026 as DUV immersion restrictions tightened. Any rebound above 25 percent would indicate regulatory loosening or a surge in permitted basic-DUV demand; a decline below 15 percent would signal further deterioration that even AI-driven EUV demand would struggle to fully offset in the near term.

**Free cash flow conversion.** ASML generated approximately €10.4 billion in trailing free cash flow as of early 2026. Monitoring quarterly FCF as a percentage of net income — ideally 90 percent or above — confirms that High-NA manufacturing scale-up and working capital build are not consuming earnings quality in ways the income statement does not fully reveal.

## The Bull/Bear Setup

The bull case into year-end 2026 rests on four simultaneous events. AI capex remains strong as hyperscalers sustain data-center build programs, keeping TSMC and SK Hynix at full utilization and maintaining EUV pull-through demand. Full-year revenue prints toward the €39–40 billion top end of guidance — achievable if Q4 2026 delivers the typical year-end acceptance flush and implies H2 revenue near €21 billion. High-NA delivers its first pilot-production acceptance revenue from a leading customer — most plausibly TSMC's N2 or successor node — validating that EXE:5200 systems are clearing customer fab-readiness criteria rather than accumulating as unrecognized conditional acceptances. And gross margin exits Q4 2026 at 53 percent or above, signaling that the High-NA cost curve is bending ahead of schedule.

The bear case is more textured. Order slowdown in H2 2026 is the primary risk: if AI hyperscalers begin a digestion phase — pausing new data-center commitments while absorbing installed capacity — leading foundries could moderate EUV scheduling orders, causing the implied backlog to erode toward €25 billion. In that scenario, 2026 revenue tracks toward the €36 billion guidance floor, and the 2030 scenario base case shrinks to a 4–5 percent CAGR that no longer supports a 40-plus forward P/E. A parallel risk is China: if the U.S. Bureau of Industry and Security extends restrictions to cover DUV service and maintenance licenses — a scenario that has been under policy discussion — ASML's installed-base management revenue from China's existing DUV fleet becomes legally uncertain, potentially removing more than €1 billion of highly recurring revenue from the model. Gross margin under this bear scenario compresses toward 51 percent or below as the high-margin China service contribution shrinks faster than High-NA ramp compensates.

## The Investor Day: Questions Premium Valuation Must Answer

ASML has not confirmed a standalone Investor Day within the frozen window, but the company is understood to host capital markets events following major product transitions. Given the EXE:5200 production ramp and the scale of the 2030 scenario ranges — €44–60 billion in revenue at 56–60 percent gross margins — a formal long-range update in late 2026 or early 2027 is the logical next disclosure milestone. Three questions must be answered to sustain the €616-plus billion market capitalization.

The first is High-NA unit economics: how many EXE:5200 systems does ASML plan to manufacture in 2027 and 2028, and at what gross margin per unit as the learning curve matures? The current 51–53 percent full-year guidance implies that High-NA cost headwinds are not yet fully absorbed; investors need a credible trajectory toward the 56 percent threshold.

The second is China's endgame. Management calibrated its 2026 guidance bandwidth to absorb further uncertainty, but the range spans roughly €4 billion of revenue risk. A formal framework for managing the China installed base under various regulatory scenarios — including a service-license restriction scenario — would meaningfully compress the uncertainty premium embedded in the stock.

The third is AI capex cycle durability. ASML's 2030 scenario implicitly assumes sustained AI infrastructure investment through the decade. An event that disaggregates AI logic demand, HBM memory demand, and mature-node demand, and stress-tests each against historical capex cycle downturns, would give investors the analytical foundation to underwrite the long-duration valuation rather than simply accepting it on faith. How CEO Christophe Fouquet and CFO Roger Dassen answer those three questions will determine whether ASML's premium multiple endures or begins its slow compression toward industrial norms.

chapters.title: 2026–2030: The AI Infrastructure Decade and ASML's Path to €44–60 Billion
chapters.body:
## The Scenario Framework

When ASML's management team articulated its 2030 financial targets, it did so in the language of scenarios rather than point forecasts — an unusual degree of epistemic humility for a company accustomed to multi-year backlog visibility. The parameters were precise enough to be useful: annual revenue of €44–60 billion at gross margins of 56–60 percent, contingent on different assumptions about semiconductor market growth and lithography intensity per wafer start. At the floor, the implied compound annual growth rate from 2025's €32.7 billion base is approximately 6 percent — modest by ASML's historical standards, consistent with the semiconductor industry's long-run revenue CAGR, and achievable without any acceleration in AI infrastructure investment beyond what was already contracted as of early 2026. At the ceiling, the implied CAGR approaches 13 percent, a rate that would require AI logic and memory capex to sustain the elevated trajectory that characterized 2024–2026 for the remainder of the decade.

The order trajectory as of the frozen snapshot date argues more persuasively for the upper half of the range. ASML ended 2025 with a record backlog of [€38.797 billion](https://www.asml.com/en/news/press-releases/2026/q4-2025-financial-results), underpinned by full-year net bookings of €28.035 billion — a figure that by itself exceeds total 2025 revenue at nearly every pure-play semiconductor equipment competitor. Q4 2025 bookings alone reached €13.158 billion, of which €7.4 billion was EUV. Against that backdrop, the floor scenario increasingly looks like a stress case rather than a base case.

## Three Demand Pillars

The 2030 framework rests on three structurally independent demand sources, each of which would individually justify a meaningful share of the projected revenue expansion.

The first and most consequential is AI logic. TSMC's N2 node entered risk production in 2025 and was moving toward volume in 2026, with the A14 and A16 angstrom-class nodes behind it. Each successive node generation requires a higher EUV layer count per wafer — N2 uses approximately 17 EUV layers versus N3's 14 — and ASML's High-NA EUV systems, with their 0.55 numerical aperture enabling single-exposure patterning at sub-8 nanometer features, become progressively more economical relative to multi-patterning workarounds as nodes shrink. Samsung Foundry's SF2 and SF1.4 nodes, and Intel Foundry's 14A process targeting 2026 risk production, each represent additional EUV intensity vectors. CEO Christophe Fouquet characterized the aggregate AI demand signal as generating "another record year" in 2025 and noted customers had displayed "notably more positive assessments of the medium-term market" as the year closed. The 2026 guidance raise — to €36–40 billion from a prior €34–39 billion range — after a single quarter of results confirmed that AI capex was not merely signaled but contracted.

The second pillar is AI memory. High-bandwidth memory has become one of the most lithography-intensive products in the semiconductor supply chain. HBM3E, deployed in Nvidia's B200 and H100 platforms, requires significantly more EUV patterning steps than standard DDR5 DRAM; HBM4 and HBM4E, scheduled for volume production in 2026–2027, will extend that trend. SK Hynix — as the dominant HBM supplier — has accelerated EUV investment at its advanced 1-beta and anticipated 1-gamma DRAM nodes, and Samsung's memory division is pursuing a parallel ramp. Each incremental EUV layer per DRAM wafer represents direct revenue for ASML at multiple points: the system sale, the optical column upgrade, and the recurring service and software revenue that follows the installed-base lifecycle.

The third pillar is mature-node DUV expansion, geographically diversified away from China. Automotive electrification, industrial automation, and sovereign chip programs — Europe's CHIPS Act equivalents, Japan's Rapidus investment, India's nascent fab ambitions — are driving demand for DUV immersion and dry systems at nodes between 28nm and 130nm. This segment will not replicate the revenue density of EUV, but it provides volume for ASML's DUV manufacturing base and seeds installed-base management revenue that compounds over decades.

## High-NA: The Decade's Swing Factor

The revenue model for High-NA EUV is perhaps the single most important variable in distinguishing the floor from ceiling scenario. ASML completed shipment of its five EXE:5000 research tools in Q1 2025 and transitioned production to the EXE:5200 from Q2 of that year. In Q1 2026, two High-NA systems contributed to over €4.1 billion of EUV revenue in the quarter alone — an early signal of how materially a single system, at an estimated €300–400 million average selling price versus roughly €180 million for the NXE:3800E, shifts quarterly revenue recognition.

| Year | Estimated High-NA Units | Revenue Contribution (€B) |
|------|------------------------|--------------------------|
| 2025 | ~5 (EXE:5000 seed) | ~1.5–2.0 |
| 2026 | ~10–12 | ~3.5–5.0 |
| 2028 | ~20–25 | ~7–10 |
| 2030 | ~25–30 | ~9–12 |

Reaching 25–30 units per year by 2030 requires customers to complete Phase 2 pilot-production qualification and commit to Phase 3 volume integration — a transition that historically takes three to five years from first tool receipt. Given that TSMC, Intel, and Samsung received their EXE:5000 systems in 2024–2025, Phase 3 volume timelines of 2027–2028 are plausible but not certain. The primary risk is process integration complexity: High-NA's anamorphic lens introduces new reticle masking challenges, and yield learning curves at each customer will dictate the pace of wafer-start commitments. A slip of 18–24 months in the Phase 3 ramp would compress the 2030 contribution by €3–4 billion and tilt the outcome toward the lower half of the scenario band.

## Installed-Base Management: The Compounding Floor

ASML's installed base exceeded 5,000 systems globally as of early 2026, growing by approximately 100–150 net new units annually. By 2030, the base is likely to approach 5,500–6,000 systems. The installed-base management segment — comprising service contracts, scanner upgrades such as the NXE:3800E's PEP-1E productivity enhancement released in Q1 2026, and Holistic Lithography software subscriptions — generated €8.2 billion in 2025, roughly 25 percent of total revenue. If revenue per installed system grows at 5–7 percent annually through expanded software attach rates and optical column refresh cycles, the segment could reach €12–14 billion by 2030, effectively doubling from 2025 levels. This matters disproportionately for the gross margin trajectory: service and software revenue carries margins structurally above the corporate average, and its growth is largely independent of new system shipment cycles.

## The Gross Margin Expansion Arithmetic

Management's 56–60 percent gross margin target for 2030 requires approximately 350–750 basis points of expansion from the 52.8 percent recorded in full-year 2025. The arithmetic across the three primary levers is as follows. First, High-NA manufacturing cost reduction: early EXE:5200 systems are produced at elevated unit cost as ASML climbs the production learning curve; as yields improve and the supply chain matures across the decade, High-NA margins should converge toward or exceed low-NA margins, contributing perhaps 150–250 basis points of gross margin lift at full ramp. Second, software and service mix: every percentage point of installed-base management as a share of revenue, at above-average margins, contributes roughly 30–50 basis points at the corporate level; a shift from 25 percent to 30 percent share would contribute 150–250 basis points. Third, DUV pricing power on upgrades: the existing China-impaired DUV installed base in non-China geographies will require ongoing upgrade investment, and ASML's lack of competition on upgrades for its own systems gives it near-complete pricing authority. The arithmetic is achievable, though the ceiling of 60 percent would require all three levers to fire simultaneously and on schedule — a scenario that should be assigned higher probability at the midpoint of the decade than at its start.

## Key Risks to the 2030 Scenario

Three risks warrant explicit probability-weighting against the base case. The most credible is an AI infrastructure digestion event — a multi-year pause in hyperscaler and cloud capex as data center buildout outruns monetizable AI workload demand. The semiconductor industry has a well-documented history of over-ordering during up-cycles; if AI inference revenue fails to justify the capital commitments of 2024–2026, a correction in 2027–2028 would compress ASML's system revenue and push the 2030 outcome toward the floor scenario. The probability is material — perhaps 25–35 percent — though the long lead times on ASML systems and the confirmed backlog as of early 2026 provide insulation through at least 2027.

The second risk — a domestic Chinese EUV breakthrough that reduces import substitution demand — is lower probability than the geopolitical discourse suggests. EUV requires a supply chain that China's indigenous semiconductor equipment industry has not credibly approached; the commercial and physical barriers are of a different order than those China has overcome in mature-node equipment. A plausible assessment places this probability below 10 percent by 2030 for any system reaching production-capable specification.

The third and most structurally significant risk is a U.S.-China decoupling that fragments ASML's global market access beyond the DUV restrictions already in place. If service revenue from ASML's existing China DUV installed base — currently permitted — were curtailed by further regulatory action, the revenue impact could be €1–2 billion annually with limited offsetting substitution. More severely, if geopolitical escalation extended to restrictions on ASML's ability to service systems in allied countries under certain trade conditions, the damage to the installed-base management revenue floor could be material. As of the frozen snapshot date, no such action was indicated, but the regulatory trajectory since 2019 has moved in one direction only.

The weight of evidence across the order backlog, the AI capex trajectory, and the High-NA ramp schedule positions the 2030 base case closer to €50–55 billion than to either extreme of the stated scenario band — a range that would imply roughly 8–11 percent CAGR from 2025, consistent with a company that has converted monopoly technology into multi-decade compounding.

## Glossary

**Backlog** — Cumulative value of customer orders received but not yet recognized as revenue. ASML's year-end 2025 backlog stood at €38.797 billion.

**DUV (Deep Ultraviolet)** — Lithography using 193nm or 248nm wavelength light. ArF immersion DUV supports multi-patterning down to sub-10nm effective resolution; sold under the TWINSCAN brand.

**EUV (Extreme Ultraviolet)** — Lithography using 13.5nm wavelength light generated by laser-driven tin plasma. Enables single-exposure patterning at resolutions unreachable by DUV.

**EXE platform** — ASML's High-NA EUV product family (EXE:5000, EXE:5200). Numerical aperture of 0.55.

**HMI** — Hermes Microvision Inc., acquired by ASML; provides e-beam wafer inspection systems.

**High-NA / Low-NA** — Numerical aperture classification for EUV systems. Low-NA (NXE platform): 0.33 NA. High-NA (EXE platform): 0.55 NA, enabling smaller feature resolution.

**Holistic Lithography** — ASML's software platform integrating scanner, mask, and metrology data to optimize patterning yield; increasingly carries recurring SaaS-like revenue.

**Installed-base management** — Service contracts, scanner upgrades, and software subscriptions across ASML's global installed base of more than 5,000 systems; contributed €8.2 billion in 2025.

**NA (Numerical Aperture)** — Optical measure of a lens system's light-gathering ability; higher NA enables finer feature resolution.

**Net bookings** — Value of new orders received in a given period, net of cancellations. ASML discontinued quarterly disclosure beginning Q2 2025.

**Node** — Shorthand for a semiconductor process generation (e.g., N3, N2), loosely correlated with minimum feature dimensions though naming conventions vary by manufacturer.

**NXE platform** — ASML's Low-NA EUV product family (NXE:3400, NXE:3600D, NXE:3800E). Workhorse of current leading-edge production.

**Reticle** — The photomask through which light is projected onto a wafer; High-NA EUV uses an anamorphic reticle format distinct from Low-NA.

**TWINSCAN** — ASML's dual-stage DUV platform architecture enabling simultaneous measurement and exposure for higher throughput.

**WpH (Wafers per Hour)** — Standard throughput metric for lithography systems. NXE:3800E reached 230 WpH with the Q1 2026 PEP-1E upgrade.

**YieldStar** — ASML's optical scatterometry metrology platform for in-line overlay and process control measurement.
